it is neither dharma nor non-dharma; it is neither identical nor different; it is neither one nor all. For what reason [is this so]?"
"For this reason, today you yourself speak of 'True Suchness as the One Mind. [You claim] it is 'one' because it relies on the one;

it is the 'One Mind of Arising and Ceasing' because it is 'one' due to its causes being many. Is this not a fault for the World-Honored One, wherein there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows?
The Buddha said, "Good man, do not speak in such a manner. Why is this? The nature of the mind is not one; it is made one by its causes."
They are conventionally designated as "one. Mental factors are not all-encompassing; because they are produced by causes that are all-encompassing, they are conventionally designated as "all.
When it is said that there is "one mind" and not "all minds," this is because the name is established according to the specific mind capable of performing a function.
...and so forth, as explained at length. These ten names collectively encompass the fundamental designations for the entire treasury of all Buddhas' teachings.
Having already explained the ten distinct names of the two dharmas, I shall next explain the distinctions between the names of the two gates. First, regarding the Mind-Reality (cittatattva)...
There are ten such [gates]: first, the gate of the Tathāgatagarbha, because it is free from confusion;
second, the gate of non-dual equality, because it is without differentiation; third, the gate of the purity of the single path, because it has no divergent branches;
fourth, the gate of non-arising and non-movement, because it is detached from karmic activity; fifth, the gate of being neither interrupted nor...
1. It is called the gate of bondage because there is no obstruction to be remedied. 2. It is called the gate of neither going nor coming because there is no ascending or descending. 3.

It is called the gate of the supramundane because it is free from the four marks [of birth, abiding, change, and cessation]. 4. It is called the gate of quiescence and tranquility because there is no movement toward anything. 5.
It is called the gate of the great universal characteristic because it is free from particular characteristics. 6. It is called True Suchness (Tathatā).
Gate. Because it is free from falsehood. These ten names collectively encompass the names of all the Dharma-treasuries of the Buddhas, the principles of equality, and the gates of the Dharma.
Next, the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind has ten names. The first is called the Gate of the Ālayavijñāna, which stores and maintains all things.
First, it is called the gate of defiled and pure phenomena. Second, it is called the gate of the Tathāgatagarbha, because it conceals the body of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-nature.
Third, it is called the gate of activation and movement, because of the continuity of karmic activity. Fourth, it is called the gate of having severance and having bondage.
1. It is called the "Gate of Possessing Obstructions" because it possesses hindrances. 2. It is called the "Gate of Having Departure and Arrival" because it has ascent and descent. 3.

It is called the "Gate of Many Diverse Aspects" because the dharmas of defilement and purity exceed the sands of the Ganges in number. 4. It is called the "Gate of the World" because it pertains to the mundane realm.

The fourth is called the gate of simultaneous revolution because the four characteristics (of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing) revolve together. The eighth is called the gate of the circulation and cessation [of saṃsāra] because it fully encompasses both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa.
The ninth is called the gate of mutual dependence and co-arising because there is no dharma that exists through self-origination.
The tenth is called the gate of arising and ceasing because it manifests the characteristic of impermanence. These ten names collectively encompass the entire treasury of all dharmas of the Buddhas.

The names of the various distinct dharma-gates have already been explained through two gates and ten specific designations. Next, the gate of the characteristics of sameness and difference is explained.
What are the characteristics of the sameness and difference between these two fundamental dharmas? The verse says:

There are three differences and two similarities; Each is distinguished by its basis, gate, and object; Because each is pervasive and the name is the same, they share the same name despite differing meanings.
The Treatise says: These two fundamental dharmas have three differences and two similarities. What are the three differences? First, the difference of basis (*āśraya*).
First, they differ in their respective bases (*āśraya*), because each Mahāyāna has its own basis. Second, they differ in their gateways (*dvāra*), because each has its own specific gateway of entry.

Third, they differ in their objects (*viṣaya*), because each takes its own respective basis as its objective support (*ālambana*). What are the two similarities? First, they are identical in pervasiveness (*vyāpti*).
Because they pervade the dharma-realm and are equal in measure; second, because their names are the same, as ten kinds of names apply to both dharmas.
Why is this so? Because the names are identical while the meanings differ. What are the characteristics of the similarities and differences between these two types of dharma-gates? The verse says:
There are seven differences and one similarity: The person, the dharma, the basis, the practice, the essence, The object, and the stage;

they differ because their names and meanings are distinct. The treatise says: These two types of expositions have seven differences and one similarity. What are the seven differences? First, the assembly of persons.

First, they differ in their nature: the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) consists solely of pure liberation, whereas the gate of arising and ceasing contains all three aggregates of sentient beings. Second, they differ in their dharmas:

the gate of True Suchness contains only those dharmas that are exclusively pure and white, whereas the gate of arising and ceasing contains all dharmas, both defiled and pure. Third, they differ in their basis.

Fourth, the practices differ because each Mahāyāna vehicle has its own basis. Within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), one takes the non-arising of a single mind and a single thought as the practice for liberation from bondage.
Within the gate of arising and ceasing, one takes the arising of arising and the ceasing of ceasing as the practice.
Fifth, the essential characteristics differ; the mind-gate of True Suchness is with its original...

Because they are equal; because the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind is distinct from its source. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "That which is quiescent extinction is called the one mind;
the one mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha. Sixth, their objects differ, as each takes its own basis as its object.
Seventh, their stages and positions differ, for [the two gates] abide in mutual interpenetration within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*). [The gate of] arising and ceasing...
Because they proceed toward and abide within the gates, how are they "identical"? It is because they are universally identical.
Why is this so? Because their names and meanings differ. Regarding the two gates, stages, and levels, which sūtras clearly explain them, and how many levels does each possess? The verse says:

In the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other sūtras, it is clearly explained that within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) there is one [aspect], while in the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) there are two, because they respectively cause confusion above and below.
Thus, the treatise says: "The positions and stages of these two gates are clearly and explicitly taught in the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other sūtras. That is to say, the Great...
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra states:
Dedication is itself the mind of faith; the mind of faith is itself the Buddha-ground; the Buddha-ground is itself the ten grounds; and the ten grounds are themselves the arousal of the bodhicitta.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* explains the divergent streams [of realization] as follows:
The tenth stage is the first stage; the first stage is the eighth stage; the ninth stage is the seventh stage, and the seventh stage is the eighth stage;
the second stage is the third stage; and the fourth stage is the fifth stage.
The third ground is the sixth ground; what sequence could there be in quiescence?
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"A one-year-old mother gave birth at once to fifty-year-old sons; those fifty-year-old sons..."
If a mother who has carried a child for one year gives birth to a man of fifty-one years, would such a great man exist, or would he not exist?
Regarding such various sūtras, how are their stages and levels established based on the reality of the mind? Within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā):
There is only the state of being exclusively disordered; there is no other state. Therefore, the verse says "only disorder.
In other sūtras, the successive progression through various states and stages is established based on the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*);
this should be carefully examined. Based on the gate of arising and ceasing, there are two kinds of states: first, the upward-facing gate; second, the [downward-facing] gate.
The lower gate. Thus, the definitive discernment of arising and ceasing within these two gates shall be explained in detail below.

As for the principle of the true suchness (*tathatā*) realized by correct wisdom within the gate of the mind’s arising and ceasing—under which gate is it subsumed? It is subsumed under the gate of arising and ceasing, because it is not a separate division of the gate of true suchness.
Furthermore, what difference is there between the true suchness of these two gates? The principle of the gate of true suchness is, in itself, the principle...

Because it is the principle (*li*). In the gate of arising and ceasing (*shengmie men*), the principle and wisdom are the principle itself. Regarding the stages and positions of these two gates, for what reason are their principles distinct?
Because one is unobstructed and the other is obstructed. This is cited as one corner [of the case]; one should observe accordingly as appropriate.
The Text says: "These two gates each comprehensively encompass all dharmas.
The Commentary says: "This refers to the gate of the Dharma that is all-inclusive and perfect.

That is to say, the Gate of True Suchness (tathatā) encompasses all dharmas, because there is not a single dharma that is not True Suchness; and the Gate of Arising and Ceasing encompasses all dharmas, because there is not..."
Because each and every dharma is neither arising nor ceasing. However, the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) cannot encompass all dharmas of the gate of arising and ceasing;

likewise, the gate of arising and ceasing cannot encompass all dharmas of the gate of True Suchness. Yet, when it is said that [the One Mind] "comprehensively encompasses all dharmas," it means it comprehensively encompasses all dharmas of the gate of arising and ceasing, and it comprehensively encompasses True Suchness.
Because all phenomena are such. Why is this? Because both gates are entirely equal, yet each remains distinct.
The original text asks: "What is the meaning of this? It replies: "Because these two gates are not separate from one another."
The Commentary states: This is the "Gate of Revealing Causes through the Formulation of Questions and Answers," because it directly presents the questions and directly provides the answers.
The Root Text says: "The True Suchness of Mind is the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-Gate of the Single Dharma-Dhātu."

The Commentary states: This is the section on the detailed exposition. Within this Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there are three gates: first, the Gate of the Fundamental Nature of True Suchness;
second, the Gate of Initiating Questions and Answers to Resolve Doubts; and third, the Gate of Provisionally Designating the Characteristics of True Suchness.
Within the first gate, there are further three gates: first, the Gate of Establishing Names; second, the Gate of Directly Expounding True Suchness...
Section on the Essential Nature. Section Three: Explaining the Names. This is the first section, meaning that names are established according to their functional capacities.
Within the single mind and *tathatā*, there are ten names each; why are the others excluded and only these names established? Because they correspond to the actual functions performed.
The remaining various names are certainly not like this, and therefore they are omitted and not established. What is the meaning of this? Mind...

One version reads "great activity" (*mahākarma*); another reads "collective activity" (*saṃgrahakarma*); and yet another reads "characteristic activity" (*lakṣaṇakarma*). Therefore, [the term] *dharma* functions as a "gate.
Since a gate is the essence (*tattva*), it is called the "essence of the dharma-gate. One should carefully examine these various distinct characteristics in their respective directions.
The Text says: "That which is called the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished.

The Commentary says: This directly explains the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) while distinguishing it from the Gate of Arising and Ceasing. It means that the dharma of True Suchness is neither born nor extinguished;
it is without birth or extinction, without abiding or change, and without non-abiding or non-change. It is not like arising and ceasing.
Dharmas arise and cease; having arising and ceasing, they abide and change. Because they possess abiding and changing, they are distinguished by the presence or absence of their characteristics.
Furthermore, it is not that [the teaching] is "no. It is not that one says "no" because it is non-existent; rather, it is "no" because it is not [what it appears to be]. Why is this so?
That *tathatā* (suchness) is "not" through a hundred negations and "not-not" through a thousand affirmations; it is neither "is" nor "is-not."
It is neither non-being nor being, for it does not abide even in non-duality.
The *Mūla* states: "All dharmas exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought. The *Śāstra* states:

"For the time being, we provisionally posit their existence to demonstrate that they are actually non-existent; that is, by means of the provisional existence of the gate of arising and ceasing, it is shown [to be empty]."
Because the reality-gate (tathatā-mukha) is in fact non-existent.
The *Běn* says: "If one is detached from mental conceptions, then there are no signs of any objective realms.
The *Lùn* says: "If one is detached from all consciousnesses of conceptual proliferation (prapañca), there are no false objective realms whatsoever."

The *Běn* (Root Text) says: "Therefore, all dharmas from the very beginning have been free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects.

The *Lùn* (Commentary) says: This is because it directly reveals that the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) possesses the characteristic of absolute transcendence; thus, [it is beyond] verbal expression, names, and the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).
How many are there for each, and what are their characteristics? The verse says:
There are five kinds of verbal expression, Two kinds of names, And ten kinds of mind-only, Because they are explained differently in the sūtras.
The treatise says: There are five kinds of verbal expression. First, verbal expression based on signs; second, verbal expression in dreams;
third, verbal expression based on false attachment; fourth, verbal expression from beginningless time; and fifth, verbal expression according to the meaning. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"Mahāmati, verbal expression based on signs arises from clinging to the various signs of form and so forth. Mahāmati, verbal expression in dreams [arises] from recollection..."
One originally experiences illusory objects; upon awakening from a dream, one realizes that [the experience] arose based on illusory objects that are not real.
Mahāmati, those who cling to verbal expression do so because they give rise to mental activity by recollecting what they have previously heard.
Mahāmati, beginningless verbal expression arises from the habitual perfuming of the seeds of affliction through clinging to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) since time without beginning.
The *Samādhi-saṃgīti Sūtra* states: Śāriputra said, “All phenomena are merely words and letters; the nature of words and letters is not the meaning itself.
Since the meaning as it truly is cannot be expressed in speech, how does the Tathāgata now teach the Dharma?
The Buddha said, “When I speak of teaching the Dharma, it is because you sentient beings speak while remaining within the cycle of birth; thus, I speak.”
It is ineffable; therefore, it is spoken of. That which I speak is speech of meaning, not of words. What sentient beings speak is speech of words, not of meaning.
That which is speech of non-meaning is entirely empty and non-existent. Words that are empty and non-existent do not express meaning.
That which does not express meaning is all false speech. That which is speech of meaning is truly empty yet not empty; emptiness is reality.
It is unreal. It does not abide in the middle between the two characteristics; the dharma that does not abide in the middle is free from the three characteristics and finds no location.
Because it is taught as suchness (tathatā), it is thus: the first four of these five "middles" are conventional expressions, and because they are false speech, they cannot speak of the truth.
The final one is an expression of reality; because it speaks according to reality, it can speak of the true principle. — Aśvaghoṣa.
The Bodhisattva, based on the preceding four points, makes this statement: "That which is free from the characteristics of verbal expression consists of two kinds of names:

first, the name consisting of individual syllables; second, the name consisting of reflected images. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding the 'body of names' (*nāmakāya*):"
That which is called "syllables" (vyañjana) is distinguished by names. From the letter *a* to the letter *ha*, these are termed the "name-body" (*nāmakāya*).
As stated in the *Dharmapada-sūtra*: "In a mirror, what is commonly spoken of as a 'reflection' is actually a name.

There are two kinds of syllables: first, syllables based on sound; second, syllables based on space. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the 'syllable-body' (*vyañjanakāya')..."
That which refers to the length and brevity of sounds, and the high and low pitch of their resonance, is called the "body of syllables" (*vyañjana-kāya*).
The *Mahā-samudra Sūtra* states that the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "Regarding what you previously asked—what is meant by the 'syllable of the space-circle' (*ākāśa-cakra-vyañjana*)?
It is like a bird flying through the sky; when its brilliant light appears, it produces ten kinds of harmonious sounds. This is the syllable of the space-circle."
One should contemplate in this manner. Thus, among these two pairs, the first type in each cannot express the profound ultimate truth, whereas the latter type in each can express that truth.
Now, based on the former category, it is said that one is "free from the marks of names.

There are ten types of mind-measure (*cittamātra*): namely, the eight consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, constitute the eight mind-measures; the ninth is the... [text fragment].
There is one consciousness-mind. Within these eleven types of consciousness-mind, among the ten [categories] mentioned above, the first nine kinds of mind do not take ultimate truth as their object.
Only the final kind of mind can take ultimate truth as its objective sphere. Here, based on the preceding nine, it is stated thus:
apart from the mind, there are no perceived objects. As the *Mūlatattva-sūtra* says: "The profoundly deep true essence is not the objective sphere of anything else."
Because it takes only its own basis as its object, the original text says:
"Ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible—it is solely the one mind; therefore, it is called True Suchness (Tathatā)."
The Commentary says: This demonstrates the merit of the three types of detachment.
That is to say, all various distinctions proceed by taking the four kinds of false discourse as their root.

All nine types of transformative theories and ten types of divergent attachments held by non-Buddhists proceed solely by taking names as their basis. [It is] the destruction of all afflictions and obstacles.
Because that which is known destroys obstacles and functions solely through the categories of mind, it is called "True Suchness" (tathatā) as being merely this single mind;
this summarizes the essence of True Suchness.
The *Mūla* says: "Because all verbal expressions are provisional designations without reality, they cannot be apprehended as they merely follow after deluded thoughts.
The *Śāstra* says: "This demonstrates the causes and conditions for the three types of detachment; that is to say, because all verbal expressions lack reality."
All provisional designations lack substantial reality. All mental consciousnesses merely follow deluded thoughts and are ultimately unattainable.
Within the ineffable principle of ultimate truth, they are shown to be devoid of the three marks. This is because false appearances and the reality of things as they are are utterly contradictory.
The Text says: "That which is called True Suchness (tathatā) is likewise without characteristics.
The Commentary says: This second transmission addresses the fault of attachment to verbal expression. It refers to ignorant sentient beings who form such attachments as:

"It is far removed from the three characteristics, it is perfected in the three virtues, and its essence is the principle of True Suchness; although it lacks provisional characteristics, it nevertheless exists."

The true nature (*dharmatā*) is spontaneously and eternally abiding, existing with certainty as a reality. By calculating it in this way, one falls into the extreme of eternalism (*śāśvata-anta*) and has no time of liberation.
Therefore, in order to dispel such a view, it is said that even *tathatā* (suchness) is without characteristics (*animitta*).
The Text says: "It is called the ultimate limit of verbal expression; by means of words, words are dispensed with. The Commentary says:

This directly demonstrates the causal conditions for the signlessness of True Suchness (*tathatā*). That is to say, all verbal expressions reach their ultimate limit in True Suchness and can go no further.
Since verbal expression is cut off, how could there be signs? Because it is beyond words, one therefore attains it through words.
It is merely the dispatching of words; thus, one is able to dispatch them. As it is said regarding the four kinds of false speech in the *Mahāvaipulya Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Kinnara-rāja Druma, saying:
'We and all this great assembly shall each, according to our own inclinations, proclaim...'"
He spoke of eighty-one kinds of approaches to the gate of non-duality.

Just as Vimalakīrti has appropriately done for us, the great assembly—expressing through speech that which transcends speech, and teaching a non-duality that is not [merely] non-dual—he has thereby removed the defilement of conventional designations.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti remained silent and said nothing. At that time, Mañjuśrī praised Vimalakīrti, saying:
Excellent, excellent! This is indeed the gateway to the true non-dual Dharma, for this is the very essence of the true non-dual Dharma.
The original text states: "This essence of True Suchness (tathatā) is not something to be discarded, because all dharmas are entirely True Suchness. Furthermore—
There is nothing that can be established, because all phenomena are identical with suchness (*tathatā*).
The treatise says: This is the section explaining names. First, the name is explained in terms of reality (*bhūta*); next, it is explained in terms of suchness. What meaning does this text clarify?
It is to demonstrate that there is no wisdom of abandonment or realization. How is this so? It means:
The arising and ceasing of the path of abandonment must depend upon the counteracting of obstacles; it cannot arise by itself.

Furthermore, within the true essence (*tattva*), there are no defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) to be eliminated, and thus there is no path of abandonment that can act as a counteragent. Why is this?
Because there is not a single phenomenon that is not the true essence. Moreover, if there were obstacles to knowledge, they would fluctuate according to the height or depth of the mind.

One might think that all stages and levels (*bhūmi*) could be established; however, because within the essence of suchness (*tathatā*) there are no distinct states that can be established, there is no means by which they could be established. Why is this?
Because there is not a single phenomenon that is not the essence of suchness.
The Text says: "One should know that all dharmas are ineffable and inconceivable; therefore, they are called True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The Commentary says: "This summarizes what has been explained above. Thus, the section on the gate of True Suchness, which is the fundamental essence, has been expounded.
The Commentary on the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra, Fascicle One.
On the first day of the sixth month in the ninth year of the Kenju era, this was collated at Ishiyama-ji using the manuscript from Kōryū-ji as the base text.
The copying of this different manuscript is finished.
The end of the first volume of the *Śrīmāhāyāna-śāstra-vyākhyā* states:
Question: If such is the meaning, how can all sentient beings accord with it and thereby attain [enlightenment]?
[The text] enters [the main discourse]. The *Śāstra* says: This explains the gate of initiating questions and answers to resolve doubts. This arises from the production of doubt leading to inquiry.
Based on what phrases does the questioner give rise to what doubts? It is said that based on the phrases "ineffable" and "inconceivable," [doubts are] produced.
There arises a doubt regarding what is difficult to conform to, based on the words of the second transmission. Consequently, there arises a doubt regarding the difficulty of attaining entry.
In this regard, one directly doubts the cause within the words that conform [to the truth], and directly doubts the fruit within the words concerning attainment of entry. Why is this?

Skillful speech gives rise to the wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) as a conforming expedient; from the wisdom born of hearing, [the wisdom born of] cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is produced.
The wisdom of reflection conforms to the skillful means for its cultivation; the wisdom born of reflection grows through the skillful means that conform to the wisdom of cultivation.
All wholesome teachings reach their limit in verbal expression, and all three types of wisdom find their consummation in mindfulness of the Dharma.
If there were no verbal expression, there would be no threefold wisdom; if there were no threefold wisdom, there would be no myriad practices. Yet, the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) is ineffable.
Therefore, there is no verbal teaching, because it cannot be conceived. Since there are no three types of wisdom, there is no means to accomplish the ten stages and the myriad practices.
Given this doubt as to what sentient beings might rely upon to gradually advance in their cultivation, he asks:
"How does one accord with [the truth] so that the causal practices can give rise to the fruition of virtue?"
If there is no cause for entry, then there can be no one who enters. If there is no one who enters, the object of entry cannot be attained.
"The one who enters" refers to the Vajra-mind, and "the object of entry" refers merely to the Vajra-ground.
Since there is no cause, by what gate could one enter the ocean of the Tathāgata’s *sārvajñā* (all-knowing wisdom)? Because of such doubts, he asks, saying: "How can one..."
One may enter [the teaching] in this way. These two questions concern doubts regarding the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) based upon the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).

That is to say, there are sentient beings who harbor such doubts: "If, within the gate of arising and ceasing, one cuts off all evils, cultivates all virtues, fulfills the causal practices, and perfects the resultant merit—would it not be impossible to say that the same applies to the gate of True Suchness? [Such a doubt would be to] negate [the teaching].
Practice virtue. One must not harbor thoughts of slandering the five ranks. Now, this intention is raised to initiate a question.
The original text says: The answer states, "If one knows that all dharmas, though spoken of, have neither speaker nor thing spoken;
and though contemplated, have neither contemplator nor object contemplated—this is called 'conformity. If one is free from both speaking and contemplating, it is called 'attaining entry.'"
The Commentary says: In their respective order, these resolve those two doubts. That which is called "conformity" (anuloma) is of two kinds:
first, conformity with arising and ceasing; second, conformity with *tathatā* (suchness). Within conformity with arising and ceasing, there are two types:
first, upward conformity, which refers to the stages from faith up to the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), serving as the skillful means that conform to the fruit of a bodhisattva.

Therefore, there are two types of downward conformity (*anuloma*). This refers to everything from the naturally pure and wondrous treasury (*prakṛtiviśuddhagarbha*) down to the first moment of faith (*śraddhā*), as these can serve as the skillful means (*upāya*) for conforming to each respective stage. As for what is called upward conformity:

through the sounds and verbal expressions of impermanence (*anitya*), the hearing-wisdom (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) regarding impermanence is produced; and by means of this hearing-wisdom regarding impermanence, [subsequent wisdoms are generated].
One develops the wisdom of reflection on impermanence. Based on the wisdom of reflection on impermanence, one develops the wisdom of cultivation regarding impermanence.
Based on the wisdom of cultivation regarding impermanence, one develops the conduct and virtue of impermanence; this is called "ascending.

As for what is called "descending conformity," based on the conduct and virtue of permanence, one develops the wisdom of cultivation regarding permanence. Based on the wisdom of cultivation regarding permanence, one develops... permanence.
The wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). From the constant wisdom of reflection, the constant wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) grows;
from the constant wisdom of hearing, constant verbal expression grows. This is called "descending. Thus, these two gates are simultaneously complete, without priority or sequence.
The distinct characteristics that obstruct knowledge will be explained in their proper place within the text. [This is] performed within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*).
Thus it is said. It is "inexpressible" because there are no sounds or verbal expressions of permanence or impermanence.
It is "unthinkable" because there are no three types of wisdom regarding permanence or impermanence.
This does not mean that there are no verbal expressions or thoughts pertaining to its own nature; rather, it is described as "inexpressible" and "unthinkable" for this reason. Therefore, it is not...
One may challenge one formulation by means of another: "Because this exists, that exists; because that exists, this exists.

If this is so, what are the characteristics of speech and thought within the gateway of *tathatā* (suchness)? It is said that there is speech, yet it is not a sound that is permanent, nor is it a sound that is impermanent.
It is such that there is neither a speaker nor anything to be spoken; it is spoken in accordance with suchness itself. Furthermore, there is...

Mindfulness is not the threefold wisdom of impermanence, nor is it the threefold wisdom of non-impermanence; rather, it is the mindfulness of the absence of both that which can be mindful and that which is to be minded—a mindfulness of quiescent extinction.
Why is this? Because within the gateway of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is no movement or direction, as all things abide in a state free from confusion.
What is meant by "conformity with True Suchness"? It means knowing that although all phenomena are spoken of, there is no such thing as a permanent discourse upon them.
It is the teaching of impermanence, the teaching of non-existence, the teaching of the inability to speak, and the teaching of that which is beyond speech.
This is called the sound that accords with *tathatā* (suchness). If it is contrary to these characteristics, it is called the sound that is inverted from *tathatā*.

Furthermore, if one knows that although all phenomena are contemplated, there is no wisdom that contemplates impermanence, no wisdom that does not contemplate impermanence, no one who contemplates, and nothing that can be contemplated—this is called contemplation that accords with cessation and tranquility.
That which is contrary to this is called inverted contemplation regarding cessation and tranquility. Thus, the section on accordance has been explained.
Next, the determination of entry into the state of doubt (*vicikitsā*). This consists of two parts: first, entry through arising and ceasing, which itself has two aspects:
(1) upward entry, which is the *Kanakavajra* stage; and (2) downward entry, which is the *Yaya* stage.
One must follow the phrases and examine them with care. Through these two aspects of *tathatā* (suchness), one enters; thus, that which is one's own basis is entered.

By what means does one enter? It is said: by dwelling in diversity. How does one enter? It is said: by being free from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) regarding discourse. Free from what kind of discourse and conceptualization?
It refers to the gate of *tathatā*, which is neither discourse nor conceptualization. Therefore, it is said: "If one is free from..."

To speak of mindfulness is called "attaining entry," because through the first transmission one attains accomplishment; through the second transmission, doubt is resolved and the principle is clarified.
Thus has been explained the section on initiating questions and answers to resolve doubts.
The text states: Furthermore, regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*), based on verbal designations and conceptual discrimination, there are two kinds of meanings. What are these two?

First is emptiness as it truly is (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*), because it can ultimately manifest reality. Second is non-emptiness as it truly is (*yathābhūta-aśūnyatā*), because it possesses its own essence, which is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharma*).

The Commentary states: This provisional explanation opens the gate of the *tathatā* (suchness) of characteristics. Within this, there are two gates: first, the gate of the *tathatā* of reality-as-emptiness;
this means that within the essence of suchness (*tathatā*), all defiled phenomena exceeding the sands of the Ganges are entirely empty, void, and non-existent.
Second, the gate of the *tathatā* of reality-as-non-emptiness; this means that within the essence of suchness...
Because all the pure dharmas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are fully complete and lacking nothing,
these two gates are each endowed with one another and are inseparable.
The text says: That which is called "emptiness" is because, from the very beginning, it has been non-associated with all defiled dharmas.
This means it is free from the differentiated characteristics of all phenomena; for these are merely the products of the deluded mind’s conceptualization.

One should know that the self-nature of True Suchness (Tathatā) is not characterized by existence, nor by non-existence, nor by that which is neither existence nor non-existence, nor by that which is neither non-existence nor non-non-existence, nor by the simultaneous presence of both existence and non-existence, nor is it a single [undifferentiated] characteristic.
It is not characterized by difference, nor is it characterized by non-identity, nor is it characterized by non-difference, nor is it characterized by both identity and difference.

To state it in summary: because all sentient beings possess a deluded mind that discriminates from moment to moment, [the nature of reality] is entirely inconsistent with this; therefore, it is said to be empty.
If one were to depart from the deluded mind, there would truly be nothing that could be called empty.
The Commentary states: Regarding this, one should recite the verses on the Profound Principle (*li-xuan-song*). As those verses say:

"Far removed from the three conventional characteristics, Perfectly complete with the three ultimate virtues; By reason of these causes and conditions, The essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is established.
Far removed from the characteristics of the four extremes, Perfectly complete with the virtues of the four dharmas."
For these reasons, the *tathatā* of characteristics is established;
all modes of fault take the three and four characteristics as their basis, while all categories of merit take the three and four virtues as their basis.
For these reasons, there is neither increase nor decrease, for they are limited to the categories of number.
Having established it in this manner, I now recite the root verses of this text. Regarding the phrase "not empty":

it is because the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is revealed to be empty of falsehood that it is called "not empty. This is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*), which is eternal, constant, and unchanging.

Because it is fully replete with pure qualities (*viśuddha-dharma*), it is termed "not empty. Furthermore, it possesses no characteristics (*nimitta*) that can be grasped, for it is free from conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
The Sphere of Experience (*viṣaya*). Because it is realized only through direct correspondence with realization (*pratyātma-adhigama*).

The Treatise says: "Because the sphere free from conceptualization is realized only through direct correspondence with realization" means that it is a realization of abiding in stillness, not a realization of directed movement.
The *Běn* says: "Regarding the arising and ceasing of the mind: because it relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is a mind that arises and ceases.

The *Lùn* says: This explains the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind. Within this, there are two gates: first, the gate of the general characteristics of the basis; second, the gate of the specific characteristics of the dependent.
Second is the gate of the distinct characteristics of that which depends [upon the fundamental nature]. This contains two layers; one should observe them through reflection and contemplation.

Within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), the single mind (*ekacitta*) serves as the basis, because within the gate of arising and ceasing, the meanings of awakening (*bodhi*) and non-awakening (*abodhi*) both take the *ālayavijñāna* as their basis.

This explains the first gate. Regarding the phrase "the arising and ceasing of the mind": it is so called because it establishes what was previously proclaimed. Regarding the phrase "based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*":

this refers to the single mind as the substratum; since that very same single mind is also termed the "gate of arising and ceasing," we shall now clearly demonstrate the gate of the *tathāgatagarbha* in accordance with the sūtras.
As for the *tathāgata’s* treasury (*garbha*), how many are there? Now, regarding the *tathāgatagarbha*:
By what are they subsumed? The verse says:
"The Tathāgatagarbha has ten aspects, because they are explained differently in various sūtras; herein, the Tathāgatagarbha is subsumed under its activities and its characteristics."
The Treatise says: There are ten kinds of *tathāgatagarbha*, because they are explained individually within the *sūtras*.
First is the *tathāgatagarbha* of the Great Dharani, because it completely encompasses all *tathāgatagarbhas*. The *Sūtra on the Inexhaustible Treasury of All Buddhas* states:
The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī: "There is a *tathāgatagarbha* named the Great Jewel, Inexhaustible, and Supreme."
The Perfect Dhāraṇī. It completely encompasses all treasuries, penetrating everything and applying to everything without exception.
Perfect and perfect; equal and equal. Among all the Tathāgata-treasuries that exist, there is none for which this is not the root.
Why is this? Because this Tathāgata-treasury is the king of Tathāgata-treasuries, the master of Tathāgata-treasuries.
The *ālaya-dhātu* (storehouse realm) is the stage of the Tathāgata-garbha. For this reason, it is called the "Great Jewel, Inexhaustible, Supreme, and Perfect Dhāraṇī Tathāgata-garbha.
What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify? It reveals the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the basis upon which the dhāraṇī-treasury relies;
whereas in other sūtras, the various Tathāgata-garbhas [discussed] are the specific [aspects] that rely upon it.

Because of its characteristics. For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*? It is because it "holds" [the Tathāgata]. Second, regarding the *tathāgatagarbha* that is far removed from transmigration and far removed from bondage:
it is pure and full. The *Tattvaprativedha-sūtra* states: "The *tathāgatagarbha* consists solely of the Awakened One and solely of Suchness (*tathatā*).
It is free from the causes of transmigration and free from the bonds of discursive cognition; it is individually pure and individually white. This is...
Therefore, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha. What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It reveals that True Suchness (tathatā) possesses no cause for delusion and no cause for awakening; it possesses no fruit of delusion and no fruit of awakening.
It is a single reality, a single suchness, consisting solely of the pure and wondrous essence of the Tathāgata. For what reason is it named the Tathāgatagarbha? That is to say:
Because it is unmixed. Third, because the Tathāgatagarbha—which possesses both the power of saṃsāra and the dharmakāya—causes [the latter] to be concealed.
As the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra states: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
it experiences suffering and pleasure, and arises and perishes together with its causes, just like an actor. What does this scriptural passage clarify?
The meaning is as follows: it reveals the arising and ceasing, the power regarding delusion and the power regarding awakening, and the manifestation of the dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
It is like a magical illusionist who, through various illusory feats, exerts power and function according to what is appropriate.
For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*? Because it causes [the true nature] to be covered; because of the fourfold suchness.

Just as with the *tathāgatagarbha*, because it is solely suchness (*tathatā*), the *Zhēnxiū qìjīng* (Sutra on True Cultivation) states: "The *tathāgatagarbha* is according to principle and according to suchness;

it is neither established nor denied, neither permanent nor impermanent. It is not that which is realized by the wisdom of the fundamental essence (*mūlaprajñā*), nor is it an object of perception for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Why? Because there is only principle, and no [dualistic] principle."
For those various reasons, what meaning does this scriptural passage clarify? It is said to reveal the principle of the true suchness (tathatā) within the gate of true suchness;
it is solely the principle itself as its own nature, not wisdom as its own nature. For what reason is it called the Tathāgatagarbha?
This means that because there is no other [cause], the Tathāgatagarbha—the true suchness of arising and ceasing—is itself neither born nor extinguished.
Yet, it is defiled by the stains of arising and ceasing. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "O Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings do not awaken to or understand this;
they cling to all phenomena, which do not abide for even a single moment, and falling into false views, they speak thus: 'The untainted dharmas [arise and cease].'"
Furthermore, it does not abide for even a single moment, because that would destroy the non-illusory *tathāgatagarbha*.
Moreover, Mahāmati, the *tathāgatagarbha* realized by the Tathāgata is not something that does not abide for even a single moment.

Mahāmati, if the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata were not to abide for even a single moment, then all noble ones (*ārya*) would not be established as noble ones. What does this scriptural passage clarify?

The meaning is as follows: it refers to the principle of the *tathatā* (suchness) within the gate of arising and ceasing, which is a dharma that is free from the marks of impermanence and is neither born nor extinguished.
For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*? It is because it is defiled;
that is to say, the six kinds of emptiness constitute the *tathāgatagarbha*, for all forms of emptiness conceal the *Tathāgata*. As the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says: "World-Honored One, emptiness..."
The Tathāgatagarbha is so called because it is separated from, liberated from, and distinct from the storehouse of all afflictions (*kleśa*).

What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify? It reveals that within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpādanirodha-mukha*), all defiled phenomena (*saṃkliṣṭadharma*) conceal the immeasurable qualities of the nature of self-characterized original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsajñāna*). For what reason are all defiled phenomena collectively termed "empty"?
That which is called all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) are like magical illusions and transformations; their essence and characteristics lack reality, and their functions are not true.
Therefore, they are termed "empty. Yet, they are able to conceal and obscure the true, true essence of the Tathāgata’s real virtues of the *dharmakāya*.

For this reason, it is called the "Tathāgata-garbha" (the Womb/Treasury of the Tathāgata), as its name is established based on its capacity to conceal the defilements. This is the first of the seven [aspects of] the non-empty Tathāgata-garbha.

Because all things are not empty, as they are permeated by emptiness. The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* states: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata-garbha is not empty, because it contains inconceivable Buddha-dharmas—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—which are inseparable, non-detached, and non-different [from it]. What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It is to reveal the self-characteristic of original enlightenment within the gate of arising and ceasing, which is fully endowed with all dharmas more numerous than the sands of the Ganges.

Regarding "merit" (*guṇa*): because it is defiled by all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśadharma*) that exceed the sands of the Ganges. For what reason? All pure phenomena (*viśuddhadharma*) are collectively termed "not empty.

That is to say, all pure phenomena are real within their own essence (*svabhāva*), their functioning is supreme and wondrous, they are far removed from the false and provisional, and they transcend artifice and deception; therefore, they are called "not empty. When they are covered by the veil of defilement, they are termed...
The *tathāgatagarbha*, when manifest, is called the *dharmakāya*; when concealed, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Its name is established based on the purity of that which is contained within it. The *Tathāgatagarbha* is able to contain [all qualities], because the intrinsically pure mind within the *avidyā-kośa* (the sheath of ignorance) is able to contain all meritorious qualities. As stated in the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta*: "The *tathāgatagarbha*..."
The essence corresponding to the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) and the dharmas of purity—these dharmas are such as they truly are, without falsehood, inseparable from, and not detached from wisdom;

they are the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas. Because this essence of the dharma corresponding to this purity has existed since the beginningless primordial limit, what meaning does this scriptural passage clarify? It is said to reveal that all sentient beings themselves...
Within the intrinsically pure mind, the three wisdoms have been fully present and the four virtues have been perfected since beginningless time, without any deficiency.

For what reason is it called the *tathāgatagarbha*? Because of the inverted mind, which neither knows nor awakens [to this reality], its name is established through the relationship between the subject and the object. Regarding the ninefold *tathāgatagarbha* encompassed by all defilements...

The *Dharmadhātunirviśeṣa-sūtra* states that because the Tathāgata-garbha is subsumed by those who have attained perfect awakening after emerging [from ignorance], it is neither increased nor decreased.

Furthermore, the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta* explains that while the Tathāgata-garbha is essentially dissociated from beginningless time, the afflictive entanglements and impure phenomena are dissociated from this beginningless state; these afflictive entanglements and impure phenomena exist only [as adventitious].
Because it is that which can be severed by the Tathāgata’s bodhi-wisdom. What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It is to reveal that the Buddha, whose initial awakening (ādikṣaya-jñāna) is perfected, is sustained by the wisdom that severs all defiled dharmas. For what reason?
It is called the *tathāgatagarbha* because it holds [all things] within itself. There are ten ways in which the *tathāgatagarbha* is concealed:
because the *dharmakāya-tathāgata* is entirely covered, hidden, and obscured by afflictions. The *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta-sūtra* states:
"The *tathāgatagarbha* is equal and constant throughout the future limit and possesses all phenomena; it is the root of all dharmas and is endowed with all dharmas."
It is endowed with all phenomena, for it neither departs from nor is liberated from worldly phenomena. What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It reveals that the single essence of the mind is equal to the *dharmadhātu* and pervades the three periods of time;
it is fully perfected, encompassing all defiled and pure phenomena, such that there is nothing it does not penetrate and nothing to which it does not reach. Furthermore, it reveals...
Within the gate of following conditions, the intrinsically pure mind is concealed and submerged within defiled phenomena because the Dharmakāya Tathāgata has not yet appeared.
Among the ten aspects of the Tathāgata, this present Tathāgatagarbha consists of its activity and its characteristics.
The Root Text says: "That which is called non-arising and non-ceasing, yet is in conjunction with arising and ceasing, being neither identical nor different, is named the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

The Commentary says: This explains the gateway of the *ālaya-vijñāna*. Although the meaning is complete, it establishes the full name by omitting the names of its constituent parts. Even though the meaning...

Because it is said that they are not yet complete. Regarding what is taught here—non-arising and non-ceasing, as well as arising and ceasing—what are the respective natures of these phenomena, and what are their boundaries? The verse says:

Comprehensively encompassing all unconditioned phenomena, it is called "non-arising and non-ceasing. Because it comprehensively encompasses all conditioned phenomena, it is called the "Treatise on Arising and Ceasing.
The commentary states: Because it comprehensively encompasses all unconditioned dharmas, it is therefore called "non-arising and non-ceasing. Not...

Because it is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the cessation of all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), and because it subsumes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), it is called "arising and ceasing" (*utpāda-nirodha*). The term "arising and ceasing" is the general characteristic of all conditioned phenomena.
Thus, regarding these two types of phenomena—conditioned and unconditioned—how many are there in each, and what are their names? The verse says:
Although the unconditioned is immeasurable, it is briefly explained as being of four kinds:
namely, suchness, fundamental awakening, initial awakening, and empty space. Although the conditioned is immeasurable, it is briefly explained as being of five kinds:
namely, fundamental ignorance and the category of the four marks.

The treatise states: There are four kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*): first, the unconditioned of suchness (*tathatā*); second, the unconditioned of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*);

third, the unconditioned of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*); and fourth, the unconditioned of empty space (*ākāśa*). There are five kinds of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*): first, the conditioning of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*);

second, the conditioning of the phase of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*); third, the conditioning of the phase of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*); fourth, the conditioning of the phase of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*); and fifth...
The characteristic of cessation is conditioned. Now, what is the essence of the four unconditioned phenomena? What are their functions? The verse says:
Each basis has two kinds, Namely, the general and the specific; As it is with their essence, so it is with their function;
One should observe them according to this explanation.

The Commentary states: Each of these four unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas has two types of bases. First, the common basis, which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, because it takes the fundamental dharma of the mind as its essence.
Second, the specific basis, which exists within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), because it takes the principle of quiescence as its essence.
The unconditioned of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*) is the specific basis; within the gate of arising and ceasing, it is spontaneous...
Because it takes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as its essence, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) has the unconditioned of space as its distinct basis.

Within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), because it takes wisdom that arises in accordance with others as its essence, the unconditioned of non-existence (*akiṃcana*) has the unconditioned of space as its distinct basis.

Within the gate of arising and ceasing, because it takes the state of having nothing whatsoever as its essence. Furthermore, the unconditioned of True Suchness (*tathatā*) has two kinds of functions: first, the universal function.

Because it gives rise to all dharmas, there is a second, specific function. Because it prevents the nature of equality from being lost, fundamental enlightenment (*mūlābodhi*) as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has two kinds of functions:
first, a universal function, because it does not abide in its own nature; second, a specific function.
Because it is non-transformative, initial enlightenment (ādikṣānti) has two kinds of unconditioned functions: first, the universal function, which follows along with delusion;
second, the specific function, which counteracts one's own faults. Space as an unconditioned phenomenon has two kinds of functions: first, the universal function.

Because desire and existence cause [beings] to exist, there are two distinct functions. Because the nature of emptiness and non-existence prevents [existence] from being lost, what is explained here refers generally to the meaning of others and specifically to the meaning of oneself.
Based on these two statements, one should extensively examine their various distinct characteristics;
when reaching the relevant passages in the text, they shall be explained in detail. What constitutes the essence of the five kinds of conditioned phenomena? Existence...
What is their function? The verse says:
Each basis has two kinds, Namely, the general and the particular; Just as it is with their essence, so it is with their function— One should observe them according to this explanation.

The Treatise says: Each of the five kinds of conditioned phenomena has two types of bases. First, the common basis: they take as their essence the single fundamental mind-dharma, which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.

Second, the distinct bases: the fundamental ignorance takes as its essence the powerful Dwelling-Stage (*sthiti-bhūmi*) within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), which serves as its specific support.
As for the conditioned phenomenon of the "characteristic of arising" (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-saṃskṛta*), it has as its distinct basis the gate of arising and ceasing.
Internally, it takes as its essence the coarse categories of defiled phenomena within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). Furthermore, fundamental ignorance has two functions:
first, a general function, which is the capacity to give rise to all defiled phenomena; second, a specific function, which acts as an obstacle wherever it reaches.

Therefore, the characteristic of arising (*jāti*) as a conditioned phenomenon has two functions: first, a universal function, which provides its power to that which precedes, follows, and is simultaneous with it;

second, a specific function, which acts as an obstacle at the point where it arrives. As it is said regarding the characteristic of arising, so it is for the characteristics of duration (*sthiti*) and change (*anyathātva*).
The characteristic of cessation (*nirodha*) as a conditioned phenomenon also has two functions: first, a universal function, which provides its power to that which follows and to itself.
Therefore, there are two distinct functions. Because they function as obstructive factors, their various distinct characteristics will be explained in detail at their respective textual locations.
For what reason is it stated thus? It is because all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena arise as a single mind, which constitutes their essence;
for it is so stated in the sūtras. That is to say, the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).

The Sūtra says: At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the ālayavijñāna possesses all dharmas and is replete with all dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges. With what do such dharmas take as their root? From where do they arise?
The Buddha said, "In this way, for all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, the place of their arising is supreme."
It is inconceivable. Why? Because within that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned, the conditioned and unconditioned dharmas are able to arise.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what is meant by 'that which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned'?
The Buddha said: "That which is neither conditioned nor unconditioned refers to..."
This is precisely the fundamental dharma of the single mind. Because it is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it can produce the conditioned;
because it is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it can produce the unconditioned. Therefore, I say that the excellence of its place of birth is inconceivable.
Furthermore, good son, it is like a secondary son who has two supports: first, a great king; second, his parents. [The same applies to] the conditioned and the unconditioned.
All dharmas are likewise thus; each has two supports, namely, the support of penetration and the support of constituent parts.
Furthermore, son of good family, it is like all grasses and trees, which have two bases: first, the great earth.
Second, regarding seeds: all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are likewise thus;
each has two bases, namely, the basis of penetration and the basis of constituent parts, as explained at length.
As for "conjunction," this is the disclosure of the distinction between the perfuming agent and the perfumed object. How is it disclosed? It is by revealing the defiled [nature].
All phenomena are purified. Because they possess either power or lack power, and because they mutually possess superiority or inferiority, we shall now explain them clearly through two gates:
first, the gate of downward transformation; second, the gate of upward transformation. Within the gate of arising and ceasing, nothing exists outside these two.
How do these two gates differ? The verse says:
When all defiled phenomena possess power and all pure phenomena lack power,
turning away from the source and descending lower and lower is called the "descending gate" (adhaḥparyāya). When all pure phenomena possess power and all defiled phenomena lack power,
returning toward the source and ascending higher and higher is called the "ascending gate" (ūrdhvaparyāya).
The treatise states: Because defiled and pure phenomena possess mutual superiority and inferiority, the two modes of transformation are established.
Now, first we shall explain the fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) of the initial downward mode of transformation.
By what phenomena is it perfumed, and at what time does it perform the act of perfuming? The verse says:
There are five kinds of that which is perfumed: namely, the single dharma-realm mind and the four kinds of unconditioned [phenomena].
Because they do not possess a beginning, middle, or end, yet they grasp at a beginning, middle, and end—as clearly explained in the sutras.
The treatise says: fundamental ignorance takes five kinds of phenomena as its objects of perfuming; namely, the single dharma-realm and...
The four unconditioned [dharmas] permeate the single dharma-realm. What are their characteristics? The verse says:
In the single dharma-realm mind, there are two kinds of mastery: Namely, the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The unconditioned is fundamental ignorance; Relying upon the first mastery, It is able to perform the work of permeation.

The Commentary states: Within the single dharma-realm of mind, there are two kinds of mastery. First is mastery over the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because it serves as the locus for conditioned phenomena.
Second is mastery over the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because it serves as the locus for unconditioned phenomena.
Fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) relies upon the former mastery to perform the activity of perfuming (*vāsana*); it does not rely upon the latter.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga-sūtra* states: "Fundamental ignorance perfumes the extent of its own basis, and not that of another's basis;
therefore, it perfumes the *tathatā*-dharma. What are the characteristics of this perfuming? The verse says:
The unconditioned dharma of *tathatā* has two kinds of functions: namely, the universal and the particular, as explained in the previous analysis.
This fundamental ignorance, relying upon the first function, is able to perform the act of perfuming; the other unconditioned dharmas are likewise so.
The Treatise says: True Suchness (*tathatā*) as an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomenon has two kinds of functions, namely the general and the particular, as previously explained.
Fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) relies upon the first function to perform the work of perfuming (*vāsanā*), and not the latter function. This is as stated regarding True Suchness.
The other three unconditioned [dharmas] are likewise; they all rely on the initial function, not the subsequent functions.

As for the duration of time when fundamental ignorance performs the act of perfuming, it is neither the beginning, nor the middle, nor the end, because it grasps the beginning, the middle, and the end simultaneously.
The *Mūlaprajñā Sūtra* states: "When great-power ignorance performs the act of perfuming, it grasps the beginning, the middle, and the end all at once."

And because it does not take anything else [as its object]. Regarding what is explained here as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed (*vāsya*), for what reason is "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) called "perfuming"?
It means that it is able to draw forth those phenomena so that they are conjoined with its own essence, never being separated from it, proceeding together and evolving simultaneously.

Therefore, they are called "the perfumers" (*kṣobhaka*). Furthermore, because those dharmas do not create obstacles, but rather follow and accord with [the perfumed], without opposition or contradiction, they are called "the perfumed" (*kṣobhya*).
This refers to the five conditioned [dharmas] as the perfumers, and the four kinds of unconditioned dharmas along with the single dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as the mind that is perfumed.
These five perfumed dharmas arrive in accordance [with the perfumers] and, together with the five perfumers, meet, harmonize, and function in concert.
They function simultaneously. Therefore, it is said that "non-arising and non-ceasing" are in harmony with "arising and ceasing.

Just as Great Ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the universal basis for the fundamental dharma of the single mind, so too should one understand that the four characteristics of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) function through the initial sovereign power to perform the work of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Just as Great Ignorance, by relying on the four unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states, is able to perform its pervasive activity, [so too do the characteristics].

Regarding the process of perfuming (*vāsanā*), the four characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) should be understood in this way. Such meanings will be clearly elucidated in their respective detailed analyses (*viniścaya*).

As for the statement that they are "neither identical nor different," this is the disclosure of the distinctions between the similarities and differences of the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That is to say, it is intended to demonstrate that within the single *dharmadhātu*-mind, there is the unconditioned sovereignty of the four kinds of [unconditioned] non-... [omitted].

Because the functions of distinct activities— the mastery over conditioned phenomena within the single dharma-realm mind (*dharmadhātu-citta*) and the penetration of the four kinds of unconditioned phenomena—

are not identical in principle, they are called "not one. This is intended to demonstrate that the mastery over conditioned phenomena and the penetration of the four kinds of unconditioned phenomena within the single dharma-realm mind, which undergoes the defilement of perfuming, are [distinct] from the perfuming agent itself.
It is called "not different" because its fivefold objective phenomena do not differ from the underlying principle.
Furthermore, it is called "not one" because the perfumed pure dharmas and the perfuming defiled dharmas are each distinct.
It is called "not different" because both the perfumer and the perfumed function within a single mind and have no other [entity]. This concludes the summary of what is termed the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
The Perfect Letter.
Having already explained the downward-turning gate, next the upward-turning gate will be explained.
To establish this upward-turning gate, the words of the sūtra text must further be set forth, as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: "At that time, the World-Honored One..."
He addressed the great assembly, saying: "O Sons of the Buddha! I recall that in the past, during the time of emergence, I came to rely upon others;
during the time of entry, others came to rely upon me. What meaning does this scriptural passage clarify?
It reveals the two modes of turning. How is this revealed? Regarding 'during the time of emergence, I came to rely upon others,' this refers to the following:"
Regarding the transformation: when others come to rely upon me during the process of entry, this is the "superior transformation. What is the meaning of this?
"I" refers to the True Suchness, the original enlightenment, the Tathāgatagarbha, and the Buddha. "Coming" refers to the sense of being perfumed by [the influence of] others.
That which is "dependent on others" turns its back on its own fundamental nature because it depends on the "other," namely ignorance.

Since this interpretation is made based on the text of this sutra, it is therefore said that non-arising and non-ceasing are in conjunction with arising and ceasing; this is the downward-turning gate (adharāvatāra-mukha).
If one wishes to establish the gate of upward transformation (*ūrdhvavivarta*), one may say that arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing are in union.
For this reason, these terms are preserved in the *Tattvārtha-śāstra*.

The fundamental intention (*āśaya*) of Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa has been clearly and sequentially elucidated thus far; he merely provides a shadowy indication by mentioning one while implying the other. Therefore:
There is no deficiency or fault; the meaning of the upward-turning gate (*ūrdhvavivarta-mukha*) is self-evident within the section on remedies (*pratipakṣa*).
Having explained the upward-turning gate, next is explained the gate of comprehensive inclusion and establishment (*saṃgraha-vyavasthāna-mukha*).
As for the various distinctions among consciousnesses, how many are there in number? In which sūtras are how many kinds of consciousness each taught? The verse says:
Within the holy teachings of the Sage, the Great Awakened One, throughout his entire life,
there are ten types of sūtras that collectively summarize his various discourses. These range from the "Single Type" as the beginning to the "Ten Types" as the conclusion,
for they are clearly and distinctly explained in the *Prakṛti-saṃgraha-sūtra* and other scriptures.
The Treatise says: Generally collecting the temporal teachings of the entire dispensation, there are ten types in total. These range from one kind of consciousness up to ten kinds of consciousness.
What are the ten distinctions of consciousness as taught in the sūtras? First, the establishment of one kind of consciousness that universally subsumes all consciousnesses;
herein there are four [subdivisions]. First is the establishment of the single universal mind-consciousness (*sarva-eka-citta-vijñāna*) which universally subsumes all consciousnesses, namely:
Because a single mental consciousness pervades these two kinds of mastery and is established therein without any instability.
As stated in the *Ekacittadharmasūtra*: At that time, Mañjuśrī, receiving the power of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, how many kinds of consciousness do you teach? What are their essential natures and characteristics? We pray that you will analyze and reveal them for us.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! For the sake of this great assembly...”
"You should inquire into this matter. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall analyze and explain it for you. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "Excellent, World-Honored One!
We wish to hear it with joy. The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "I establish only one consciousness; all other consciousnesses are not established. Why is this so?"
What is this? Regarding the "one kind of consciousness": it consists of many individual consciousnesses.
This consciousness possesses various powers capable of producing all various names and designations, yet it remains a single consciousness; ultimately, there is no other dharma.

For this reason, I say that while one kind of consciousness is established, the remaining consciousnesses are not so established. Second, the *ālaya-vijñāna* is established as the comprehensive synthesis.

Regarding the various consciousnesses: it is said that the *ālayavijñāna* possesses both the sense of being obstructed and the sense of being unobstructed, because there is nothing it does not encompass.
As the *Ālayavijñāna-sūtra* states: At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what is meant by 'thoroughly penetrating the consciousness of universal characteristics' (*saṃgraha-lakṣaṇa-vijñāna*)? For what reason is it so named?"

As for the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "That which thoroughly penetrates the universal characteristic is the ālayavijñāna.
This consciousness possesses both obstructed and non-obstructed phenomena; it contains all dharmas and is fully equipped with all dharmas.
Just as the great ocean serves as the universal characteristic name for water, waves, and so forth, by this principle it is so named."
General Characteristics: Third, the establishment of the manas-vijñāna (mind-consciousness) as that which universally subsumes all consciousnesses.
This is because the manas-vijñāna is endowed with eleven types of meanings, such that there is nothing it does not encompass. As the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra* (or *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*) clearly states:
"Although various mental consciousnesses are immeasurable in number, they are merely the transformations of the manas; there is no other dharma. Why is this? It is because this manas-vijñāna...

It is endowed with eleven kinds of meanings because there is nothing it does not perform. Fourth, a single mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is established to comprehensively subsume all consciousnesses;
that is to say, the mental consciousness possesses seven kinds of transformative mastery, according to its capacity to rely upon various objects.

The Buddha replied, "The Buddhas and Tathāgatas always employ a single awakening..."

In this treatise, it is stated as follows: that which is neither identical to nor different from the union of the unborn and undying with the born and dying is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*. This consciousness has two meanings:

"The suchness of mind (*citta-tathatā*) is the essence of the single Dharma-realm, the great universal characteristic Dharma-gate. That is to say, the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished.
