Thus, there are no characteristics of any objective realm. Therefore, all phenomena from the very beginning are free from the characteristic of verbal expression, free from the characteristic of names and words, and free from the characteristic of mental objects; they are ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible.
Being solely this one mind, it is called *tathatā* (Suchness). [From the Section on the Determination of the Great Meaning of Self-Characteristics.]
Based on this teaching, from the very beginning, all merits have been spontaneously fulfilled by their own nature.
This is because the essence itself possesses the meaning of the great radiance of wisdom, and so forth, up to the meaning of being fully complete with nothing lacking.
It is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and is also called the *tathāgata-dharmakāya*. Because these [attributes] appear to be contradictory, an objection is raised.
The original text states: "The answer is: although these various meanings of merit truly exist, they possess no marks of differentiation;
they are equal and of one flavor, being solely *tathatā* (suchness)."
The Commentary states: This "Gate of Extensive Explanation through Arousing Inquiry" consists of two gates: first, the general aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā*);
second, the general aspect of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*). This [present section] concerns the general aspect of True Suchness.

Although it is stated within the gate of the great significance of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that it possesses various virtues exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges, these are merely the scope and measure of the gate of Arising and Ceasing; they are not [the nature of] True Suchness itself.

Just as with a gate, within the gate of true suchness (*tathatā*) there are no marks of differentiation; it is perfectly equal and uniform, a single mark and a single flavor, wherein only true suchness alone remains because it is the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). For this reason, there is no fault of contradiction.
The Text says: "What is the meaning of this? Because it is without discrimination and is free from the marks of discrimination, it is therefore non-dual.

The Commentary says: This provides the causal basis for resolving doubts; it clarifies that within the Gate of True Suchness (tathatā), there is only sameness and sameness, and no difference or distinction.
The Text says: "Furthermore, by what principle can their distinctions be explained?

The Commentary says: This explains the general nature of arising and ceasing. Within this, there are two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. These are presented in both detailed and abbreviated forms.
The second round of questions and answers differs from this first round. That is to say:

if all phenomena have been, from the very beginning, perfectly equal, of one flavor and one characteristic, existing solely as the ultimate truth without dual substance, then what phenomenon could there be that is not equal, such that it might serve as a basis for establishing distinctions? This is the presentation of an alternative formulation.

This is a point of doubt regarding alternative interpretations. The *Benji* (Original Text) states: "It is shown by relying on the marks of arising and ceasing within the *karmic consciousness* (*ye-shi*).

The *Lun* (Treatise) states: "This is the general answer; it means that within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there are no defiled dharmas exceeding those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

It takes that which is to be governed as incapable of governing it. Taking all pure dharmas, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, as its counter-measure, it is for this reason that within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) it is said: "All dharmas are equal and equal."
It is of one flavor and one characteristic, possessing no dual nature and so forth.

Nevertheless, within this gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), the defiled phenomena to be remedied are immeasurable and boundless, and the pure phenomena that serve as the remedies are likewise immeasurable and boundless.

For this reason, it is said within the gate of arising and ceasing that the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) is endowed with various virtues, immeasurable and boundless, exceeding the sands of the Ganges.
It is like sand and so forth; this is the general meaning. Next, an explanation shall be provided through a detailed and separate exposition.

That which is called the "basis" (*āśraya*) is the fundamental stage of ignorance (*mūla-avidyā-āvasthā-bhūmi*), for it is the basis upon which all defiled phenomena depend. That which is called "action" (*karma*) refers to the characteristic of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*).

That which is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the evolving consciousnesses and so forth. The characteristic of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the gate— *Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be an incomplete heading or transition.*

This is a general designation. As for what is called "demonstrating" (*śāsana*), it refers to demonstrating by way of contrast. Within this context, the character "with" (*yǐ*) should be extended to apply to the three characters [of the title].
This is because the arising of the merits of these three dharmas must have a causal basis.
The *Mūla* says: "How is this shown? The *Śāstra* says:
"This is the section of detailed exposition. It is of two kinds: first, the question; second, the answer.
Herein, one should know that the question is brief while the answer is extensive. 'How is this shown? is a critical inquiry—that is, an inquiry into its underlying cause."
Therefore, the *Běn* (Root Text) states: "Because all phenomena are fundamentally only mind, there is in reality no thought.
The *Lùn* (Commentary) states: This direct answer consists of three parts: first, the correct principle of our own school; second, heterodox practices that are not the Way.

Third is the correspondence regarding the measure of what is fully raised; this is the first [point]. That is to say, the dharma-nature from time immemorial is solely the one mind, for there is not a single dharma that is not mind.
The Text says: "There is a deluded mind; through non-awakening, thoughts arise, and one perceives various objective realms; therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

The Commentary says: "This is not a mere deviation from the Path; rather, it refers to the collective enumeration of all the stages of abiding in ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) throughout the fundamental [stages]."

The text says: "The nature of the mind is without arising; this is precisely the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom. If the mind gives rise to views, then there is the characteristic of non-seeing.
When the nature of the mind is free from views, this is precisely the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm.
If the mind has movement, it is not true cognition; it lacks self-nature, and is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure. It is a state of feverish affliction and decay."
If there were change, then there would be no sovereignty.
The treatise states: This directly reveals the complete enumeration of the distinctions of counterparts and measures as explained above.

Within the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), regarding each of the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*) of merit, what faults or afflictions do they respectively depend upon for observation? It is by taking these as counterparts that they are established and manifested.
It is shown as follows: namely, the perfuming of fundamental ignorance upon the ocean of the one mind gives rise to various consciousnesses such as karma.
This obscures the light of the true knowledge of prajñā and increases the darkness of delusion and confusion.
This is precisely the measure of the realm of non-awakening ignorance; in contrast to this, the nature of the one mind is quiescent extinction.
It is without arising, for it is the meaning of the light of great wisdom. As for the second quality:
when such a deluded mind gives rise to views and perceives objects, it revolves exclusively within a realm of falsehood and is unable to penetrate the true realm.
Why is this? Because truth and falsehood are mutually contradictory and do not accord. As the original text says: "If the mind gives rise to views..."
This is because there is the characteristic of non-seeing. The following clarifies the meaning of universal observation.
Since the true mind is free from the turning of views, it penetrates all phenomena; there is nowhere it does not reach, nowhere it does not accord with, and nowhere it does not exhaust.
Why is this so? Because true wisdom and vision are free from the extreme views of the seer and the seen, just like the original nature of the mind.
It is free from views, because it is the meaning of universally illuminating the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As for the third virtue:

if the mind possesses the characteristic of movement and fluctuation, this is due to the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, false movement is contrasted with illumination.
The nature of the mind is quiescent and free from agitation. It is upright and possesses a non-perverted understanding;
this is precisely the illumination of true wisdom. It accords with principle and establishes its manifestations without error. As it was originally so, if the mind were to move...
Because it is not true cognition. As for the fourth quality: it refers to the fact that false phenomena have been without intrinsic nature since beginningless time;
this is established and revealed as a counterpoint to [the former] as the primordially existing merit of self-nature purity.

This is because, as in the original state, they lack intrinsic nature. As for the fifth quality: it refers to the fact that false phenomena are subject to the transitions of the four marks [of conditioned existence].
Therefore, it is impermanent. Because it functions in conjunction with the three kinds of suffering, it is not blissful. Because the two kinds of sovereignty are absent, it is not self.

Because the single path of purification is absent, it is not pure. These four defects serve as the counter-measures against which the four kinds of virtues are established and revealed within the essence of original enlightenment (mūla-awakening).
As the root text states: "It is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure."
Therefore, the sixth quality is as follows: because false dharmas incinerate the true mind, it is called "heat" (*uṣṇa*).
Furthermore, because it vexes and disturbs all sentient beings, it is called "affliction" (*paritāpa*). It destroys and alters virtuous qualities, causing them not to arise.
Therefore, there is decay and change. Because of this fact, all sentient beings do not attain sovereignty; for this reason, they are also called "lacking sovereignty.
By observing this matter as its counterpart, the qualities of coolness, immutability, and sovereignty are established and revealed.
As the original text states: because of the affliction of heat and decay, there is a lack of sovereignty.
The text says: "Up to and including the sense of being possessed of delusory defilements exceeding the sands of the Ganges;
because this meaning exists, when the nature of the mind is unmoving, there is the manifestation of the characteristics and meanings of various pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges."
The Commentary states: This demonstrates the meaning of the characteristic of boundless merit.
That is to say, because the defiled phenomena that are to be countered are immeasurable and innumerable, the pure phenomena that serve as their antidotes are likewise immeasurable and boundless.
The Text says: "If the mind arises and further perceives prior dharmas as objects of recollection, then there is something lacking.
Such pure dharmas and immeasurable merits are themselves the one mind; there is nothing further to be recollected. Therefore, being complete, it is called the Dharmakāya, the Tathāgata-garbha."

The Commentary states: This refers to the perfection of the qualities of this bond. That is to say, if the single dharma of mind possessed the characteristic of movement and fluctuation, what further object could it perceive?
Because there would be a distinction between the perceiving mind and the perceived object, the merits of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*) would not be perfected.
Although the virtues of the fundamental nature exceed the sands of the Ganges, they are solely the measure of the one mind.
Ultimately, there is no duality of essence. Why is this so? Because all such virtues are each indivisible in their essence, being equal in measure within the single *dharmadhātu*.

Therefore, the self-nature of perfected qualities is eternally and fully present throughout both the states of bondage and liberation; it is called the *dharmakāya* and is also termed the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Regarding the determination of the equality of the number of defilements and purities, upon which sūtra is this explained?
It is as stated in the *Mañjuśrī-kauśalyopāya-sadṛśa-dṛṣṭānta-mahādhāraṇī-sūtra*:
At that time, Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, spoke the uddāna, saying in verse:
For example, like the *ajita-canaśīti* tree, its fruits are innumerable;
though their external forms appear as ten or more, the quantities of defilement and purity are likewise equal. One should understand it thus:
by relying on this analogy, the practitioner may comprehend the principles of the real and the delusive.
The text of this sutra is intended to demonstrate that the provisional depends upon the real, and that the conventional relies upon the false;

there is no such thing as an independent, self-established dharma. What is called "manifestation" refers to the metaphorical nature of false dharmas; these false and provisional things lack reality, just as a fruit has no core within its outer shell.
That which is called "real" refers to that which is analogous to the true Dharma; it is truly real and without artifice, just as [the seed] exists within the fruit.
What are the ten kinds of equality? First, equality of number expressing reality, because it accords with the corresponding number. Second, equality of object expressing reality.

1. They manifest as real through their fine powder, because it is equal in quantity with no difference. 2. They manifest as real through their weight, because when weighed, there is ultimately no difference in lightness or heaviness.

3. They manifest as real through their color, because when compared, they are the same white color. 4. They manifest as real through their fragrance, because when perfumed, their fragrances are equal.
5. They manifest as real through their taste, because when eaten, there is no difference. 6. They manifest as real through their touch.

1. Equal in manifesting reality, because there is no distinction between the body and so forth that they touch. 2. Eight fundamental equalities in manifesting reality, because they emerge from the same tree. 3.

Nine simultaneous equalities in manifesting reality, because they occur at one time without before or after. 4. Ten identical equalities in manifesting reality, because they ultimately have a single flavor.
The application of the analogy to the dharma is clear in its exposition of the characteristics; therefore, it need not be explained again.
Furthermore, if those of dull faculties do not comprehend this matter, they should understand the intended meaning through the analogy of the darkness of merit.

The text says: Furthermore, as for the functioning of True Suchness (tathatā), it refers to the Buddhas and Tathāgatas who, while originally on the causal ground, gave rise to great compassion and cultivated the various pāramitās.

They gathered in and transformed sentient beings by establishing great vows, desiring to deliver all beings within the realm of sentient beings without exception, and not limited by the number of kalpas, continuing until the end of the future, regarding all sentient beings as themselves.
Because of the body. The treatise says: Within this section on the gate of the great meaning, there are six gates in themselves: first, the gate of inexhaustible original vows;

second, the gate of detachment from marks and non-attachment; third, the gate of the equality of subject and object; fourth, the gate of manifesting response through signlessness; fifth, following... [text continues]
The Gate of Seeing the Coarse and Subtle; the Gate of Resolving Doubts through Six Question-and-Answer Sessions. This is the first gate.
Because the *śuddha-saṃnāha-āśaya* (pure resolute intention) is vast, perfect, and boundless:

it refers to the Tathāgatas’ [vows] throughout immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and unfathomable *rajas-kalpas* (dust-atoms of eons), as numerous as the dust-atoms in the worlds of the ten directions.
He possesses an ocean of great compassion of vast magnitude. He cultivates an ocean of causes for the Great Perfection as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions.
He gathers an ocean of all sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions.
He establishes an ocean of vast vows as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions. He accomplishes [an ocean] as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions.
Because it is the ocean of the fruit of Great Sovereignty (*maheśvara*). Why is this so? Because one knows, according to reality, the meaning of a single, non-differentiated continuity.
The original text says: "And yet, one does not grasp at the marks of sentient beings. What is the meaning of this? It means that one knows all sentient beings according to reality.
"Birth and one's own self are equal to *tathatā* (suchness).

The Commentary states: This is the gate of detachment from signs and non-attachment; it means that within all activities, one remains far removed from what is done and does not give rise to attachment.
That is to say, although all Tathāgatas manifest immeasurable and boundless great compassion to gather and transform all beings, [they remain detached].
[They] gather in sentient beings; yet among all Tathāgatas, there is not a single Buddha who gathers sentient beings.

Why is this? Because they know, as it truly is, that all sentient beings and their own selves are nothing other than the single True Suchness (tathatā) and the single Dharma-body (dharmakāya), which neither increase nor decrease and are without distinction.
The text states: "By means of such great wisdom of skillful means, one eliminates ignorance and perceives the fundamental Dharma-body.
Spontaneously, there arise inconceivable karmic activities and various functions, which are equal to True Suchness and pervade all places."

The treatise says: This is the gate of the equality of subject and object. It means that the essence and function, and the principle and wisdom of both person and phenomena are equal, because they are without differentiation.

That is to say, the three bodies—the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body—as well as the two principles of the real-real and the provisional-provisional, are an equal single entity, because they are without differentiation.
Furthermore, the fundamental body of self-nature and the derivative bodies of its branches are an equal single entity.
Because they are without distinction, one can realize correct wisdom; that which is realized is suchness, equal and of a single essence, because it is without distinction.
Because it is a single essence, there are not two essences; because there are not two essences, there is also no single essence.
Since there is neither two nor one, there is also not "no-ness. For this reason, the natural nature is spontaneously endowed with all virtues. It does not...
Relying on the power of another, a profoundly deep and most sublime sūtra states:
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "What is meant by 'the various and distinct characteristics,' and what is meant by 'the identical and identical characteristics'? The Buddha said:
That which is called the characteristic of difference and difference is ignorance (*avidyā*). That which is called the characteristic of sameness and sameness is the dharma of clarity (*vidyā*).
These two dharmas are like the two horns of an ox; they are characteristics of mutual opposition, not a substance that is dissolved or extinguished.
They are like two voids that are utterly severed. Therefore, these two dharmas are called "the non-contemplation of false dharmas.
At this point, Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what is meant by 'the non-contemplation of false dharmas'? Can its characteristics be described, or can they not? By what gate should one approach it?"
"Is it through awakening and knowledge? At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"In the ocean of all my sūtras, I have spoken thus: 'That which is different is ignorance; that which is identical is the dharma of illumination.
This was spoken as a provisional teaching for the sake of delivering and liberating foolish, deluded ordinary beings. But today, for your sake, I speak these words of ultimate truth. Mañjuśrī—
As the Honored One said: "For those who do not contemplate false dharmas, difference returns to sameness; sameness returns to emptiness;
emptiness returns to cessation. This is explained at length.

The text says: Furthermore, there is no characteristic of utility to be found. Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess only a body that is the characteristic of wisdom of the Dharma-body;
they are the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and have no sphere of worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya), being free from all conditioned activity.
It is simply because sentient beings gain benefit according to their respective perceptions and hearing that it is called "function.
The treatise says: This manifestation of the signless gate is the body of self-nature; it is empty, quiescent, and formless, yet it can manifest all forms.
It is like a rabbit’s horn, which is empty and non-existent in its own substance, yet is perfectly capable of producing all horns. Thus it is said of the Dharma:
The Buddha-body is solely one-by-one; it is solely quiescent-quiescent. Yet it is neither one-by-one nor quiescent-quiescent.
It is where the movements of the mind cease and the path of language is cut off. It is the extinction of extinction and the severance of severance, because it is "A" acting as "A.
Why is this so? Because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess only their own self and no other body, yet sentient beings see and hear [them].
Benefit: One obtains benefit within the measure of one’s own mind, for there is no deficiency within the body of the Dharma-nature (*dharmakāya*).

The original text states: "This function is of two kinds. What are the two? The first is that which is seen by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles based on the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects);
this is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). Because they do not know that it is manifested by the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), they see it as coming from the outside."
"Come. Because one cannot fully know the limits of form (rūpa), the treatise says:
This follows the gates of coarse and subtle. There are two such gates: first, the gate of the distinctions in the characteristics of the functions of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body);
second, the gate of the distinctions in the characteristics of the functions of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body). This is the first gate, namely, all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)."
The followers of the Two Vehicles cannot fully comprehend that all phenomena are the measure of the single mind, because this is a most profound tenet.

Relying on pervasive conceptualization and the consciousness of deluded thoughts, they perceive the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*, interpreting them as external objects; thus, they are unable to penetrate [this truth].
There is no fixed boundary, for it transforms part by part.

The original text states: "The second is that which relies on the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*). This refers to what is perceived by the minds of Bodhisattvas from their first aspiration up to the ultimate stage of Bodhisattvahood;
this is called the Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*). This body possesses immeasurable forms, and these forms possess immeasurable [attributes]."

Regarding its marks: the marks possess immeasurable secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). The fruits upon which they rely are likewise immeasurable, featuring various adornments that, according to what is manifested, are boundless and inexhaustible.
Free from the marks of limitation, they are able to constantly sustain and maintain themselves, neither decaying nor being lost, as appropriate to each case.
The Commentary states: This second gate refers to all Bodhisattvas from those at the stage of *daśabhūmi-avakalpanā* (ten-fold understanding) up to the *vajra*-stage.

Because the profound tenet is that they clearly and thoroughly realize all phenomena (*dharma*) as being solely the measure of the single mind (*cittamātra*), they perceive the Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya-buddha*) based upon their *karmic-consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) and form the understanding of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
This is because they have realized that there is no boundary between the environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Why is this?
In the chapter on the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), it is stated that one perceives that Buddha by relying on the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects).

In the chapter on the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), it is stated that one perceives that Buddha by relying on the *karma-vijñāna* (consciousness of karma). This is intended to demonstrate that the perceived bodies of the Buddha vary in their coarseness or subtlety according to the coarseness or subtlety of the respective consciousnesses.
The text states: "Such merits are all accomplished through the permeation of the outflow-free practices of the various pāramitās and through inconceivable permeation;
because they are fully endowed with immeasurable marks of bliss, they are called 'retribution'."
The Treatise says: This demonstrates the distinct characteristics of retribution (*vipāka*). As for what is called "retribution":

when there is a superior and sublime cause that results in the fruit of extreme bliss—being spontaneously sovereign, definitively at peace, and far removed from the marks of suffering—it is therefore termed "retribution."
The text states: Furthermore, that which is perceived by ordinary beings is coarse form (*rūpa*). According to the six realms of existence, what they perceive differs;
it consists of various distinct categories that do not possess the characteristics of experiencing pleasure. Therefore, it is said to be "corresponding" (*yìng*).

The treatise states: That which is called "the Responsive" (nirmāṇakāya) conforms to the capacities and faculties of sentient beings without contradiction; it manifests according to time, place, and realm of rebirth.
Because its characteristics are not those of [intrinsic] bliss, it is named "the Responsive."

The text says: Furthermore, as for what is seen by a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment: because they deeply delight in and have faith in the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness), they see it only partially;
they know that such matters as the adornment of its physical forms are without coming or going, and are free from all limitations.

It manifests solely in dependence upon the mind and does not depart from True Suchness (*tathatā*). Nevertheless, this bodhisattva still engages in conceptual discrimination because they have not yet entered the stage of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The treatise states: This is further explained in detail to clarify what was previously stated; namely, that in each respective stage, one perceives the Buddha individually.

This is because there is a distinction between increase and decrease. What is the meaning of this? If Bodhisattvas at the stage of the three levels of worthiness (triyāna-śaikṣa) perceive the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) due to their faith in True Suchness (tathatā), they contemplate and know that its physical characteristics are without limit or measure.

Nevertheless, these Bodhisattvas are unable to free themselves from the mind of conceptual discrimination (vikalpa). Why is this? Because they have not yet attained entry into the stage of True Suchness.

The text states: "If one attains a pure mind, that which is perceived becomes subtle and wondrous, and its function becomes increasingly superior, until reaching the ultimate vision at the completion of the Bodhisattva stages."
The Commentary says: For those Bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages, they proceed toward ultimate excellence in their respective order.

The Original Text says: If one is detached from the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), then there is no seeing of appearances; for within the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas, there are no mutual perceptions of self and other or of material forms.

The treatise says: If, within the state of Buddhahood, the fundamental seeds of the karmic consciousness do not exist, then that which perceives and that which is perceived are likewise empty and non-existent.
Why is this so? Because for all Buddhas, True Suchness and True Suchness are perfectly equal and identical.
The Dharmakāya is equal and perfectly equal. It is without "this" and without "that"; without self and without other;

without large and without small; without high and without low; without non-existence and without existence. All conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) has utterly ceased, and even deliberative cognition is empty.
There is only the Great Emptiness, the fundamental wisdom of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Clad in the *cakrākṣarī-śāntati* garment, [it abides] within the *kāñcī-tārā*.
The Palace of Ma (Māyā). The *svabhāvakāya* (Self-Nature Body) sits [there], for it exists alone, solitary, and non-dual.
The original text says: Question: If the *dharmakāya* (Dharma Body) of all Buddhas is free from the marks of form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*), how can it manifest the marks of form?
The Treatise says: This section on resolving doubts through question and answer contains two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. This is the question.

As for what is meant by "questioning," it refers to raising a doubt as follows: "Regarding the true essence of the Dharmakāya—profoundly serene and beyond conceptual thought, utterly tranquil and termed 'cessation'—by whom do its physical forms and karmic activities arise? How can that which is signless manifest in response? This must be definitively resolved."
In the *Vibhaṅga*, it is stated as follows: "The Dharma-body is without marks, yet it can manifest material forms. If it can manifest various material forms, they are ineffable.
The Dharma-body is empty and quiescent, transcending the realm of form and image. It is because of such doubts that [this was said].
The text says: The answer is that because this very Dharmakāya is the substance of form, it is able to manifest as form.
That is to say, from the very beginning, form and mind have been non-dual.
The Commentary states: This response consists of five gates. First, the gate of the manifestation of the form-aspect of the Dharmakāya;
second, the gate of manifesting the form-aspect of the Jñānakāya; third, the gate of manifesting the form-aspect of the Dharmakāya;
fourth, the gate of vast, perfect, and boundless [pervasiveness]; fifth, the gate of inconceivable excellence. This is the first gate: the intrinsic nature of the Dharma.
The body can manifest as physical form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) and serves as its basis; it skillfully produces physical forms because they are without obstruction.

Why is this so? Because the dependent dharmas of form and the supporting dharmas of mind have been equal and identical from beginningless time, possessing no dual nature, for they are but the single measure of mind (*citta-mātra*).
The *Ben* (Root Text) says: "Because the nature of form is itself wisdom, the substance of form is formless; it is therefore called the 'Wisdom Body' (*jñānakāya*). The *Lun* (Commentary) says:
"This reveals the gate of the characteristics of the Wisdom Body. Because form is subsumed by wisdom, there is not a single instance of form that is not wisdom;
therefore, it is called the 'Wisdom Body.'"
The Root Text says: "Because the nature of wisdom is identical to form, it is called the Dharma-body.

There is. By virtue of their great significance, these three great elements must possess substantial characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, within each of the first three, there is one of the second;

The text states: Furthermore, it demonstrates how one enters the gate of True Suchness from the gate of Arising and Ceasing.

There is none. This is because both the subject that empties and the object that is emptied are themselves empty, serving as the gateway for entering the equality of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The text says: "It is like a person who, because of delusion, mistakes the east for the west; yet the directions themselves do not actually change. Sentient beings are likewise:

The ground-abidings give rise to various defiled dharmas as their retinue, which conceal the immeasurable, untainted nature of pure wisdom and clarity.

The *Lun* (Commentary) says: This clarifies the characteristics of obtaining benefit. That is to say, there are sentient beings who understand the dharmas of the mind;

Entry. Because there is no compliance and no attainment, there is no entry.

there is nothing else. This is because these heterodox attachments rely upon this very root.

The Root Text says: "Regarding the view of a self in persons (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), it is said that there are five types based on ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

The Commentary says: This demonstrates that there are two gates for the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*) against the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*). First, a general presentation and general explanation; second, a detailed and individual exposition.
This is the first [gate], which directly serves as a counteractive measure against those in the group of the wrongly fixed (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*) and the group of the unfixed (*aniyata-rāśi*).
This is for the purpose of generating a sublime understanding regarding the faults of the erroneous attachments of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

It awaits [conditions]. It perceives characteristics in response to form; it is that which is known by the mental ground (*manobhūmi*); it takes form as its nature through transformation; and it is comprised within the *parikalpita* (imagined) nature.

Therefore, it is said to cause the mind to arise and perish. How could this be the same as the Dharma-body, which is non-confrontational and realized by correct gnosis (*samyagjñāna*), wherein both the perceived characteristic (*nimitta*) and the perceiving aspect (*lakṣaṇa*) have vanished?
Regarding "all forms and so forth": form is fundamentally mind; it is non-existent because its characteristic is emptiness.
Regarding "so-called all objects and so forth": this precisely clarifies that the two types—form and emptiness—are called "all objects.

Its essence and function are all-pervasive, and its nature and wisdom are indestructible; therefore, it is said that it is not like empty space.
The text states: "Second, one hears it said in the sūtras that all worldly phenomena are ultimately empty in essence, and even the dharmas of nirvāṇa and true suchness are ultimately empty.

The treatise says: It is explained that the world is "empty" because the essence and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all worldly phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely without utility and are not real.

Regarding the phrase "from the very beginning," this precisely clarifies the distinction between the two types of emptiness. If [it refers to] worldly phenomena...
It is like flowers in the sky; because its nature is inherently empty and non-existent, it is said that from beginning to end it is itself empty.
Because the essence of true suchness (*tathatā*) and nirvāṇa transcends all marks, it is said to be free from all marks.

The *Lun* (Commentary) says: Regarding the phrase "because they do not understand that [the teaching] is for the purpose of destroying attachments," the *Sūtra of Examining the Ground* states: "However, all sentient beings..."
Beings constantly delight in discrimination and cling to all phenomena; because of their inverted false imaginings, they undergo birth and death.

Therefore, the Tathāgata, wishing to cause them to abandon such discriminating and clinging thoughts, teaches that all worldly phenomena are ultimately empty of essence and non-existent, and even all supramundane phenomena are likewise so.

Ultimately, its essence is empty and non-existent. This is stated from the perspective of those who are deluded. Furthermore, it is because they do not understand that the two emptinesses—the ultimate and the conventional—are entirely distinct;
they claim that suchness and nirvana are identical to worldly phenomena, being merely empty and non-existent.
The *Mūla* says: "What is the counteractive measure? It clarifies that the self-substance of the *tathatā*-dharmakāya is not empty, for it is fully endowed with immeasurable intrinsic merits.

The original text states: "Third, when hearing the Sūtras say that the Tathāgatagarbha neither increases nor decreases, and that its substance is fully endowed with all dharmas of merit..."

They encounter various Buddhas, draw near to them, make offerings, and practice with faith.
The Commentary says: This is the gate that reveals the efficacy of practice; it refers to sentient beings of the indeterminate group.
One believes in the causes and conditions of karmic retribution; there appears to be the principle of the non-emptiness of the harmony of causes and conditions.

Therefore, one recognizes the faults of the ten unwholesome actions and gives rise to the intention not to perform them; one contemplates the merits of the ten wholesome actions and gives rise to the intention to perform them.
One grows weary of the ground of bondage and seeks the realm of liberation; because one gradually departs from it and proceeds toward Bodhi, the original text says:
"After ten thousand kalpas, the mind of faith is perfected."
The Treatise says: This is the section on the duration of the accomplishment of this faith.
It is intended to reveal the distinctions in the temporal proximity or distance of the accomplishment of faith. Within this very section, fifteen sūtras each provide different explanations.
First, the *Sūtra on All Dharmas Having No Master as Their Cause and Condition* states: At that time, Mañjuśrī...
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, from the stage of being bound by all fetters,

how much time must pass for those in the indeterminate group who practice all paths before they fully accomplish the ten kinds of faith, gradually advance to a superior state, and enter the stage of non-retrogression?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One told Mañjuśrī, "Good son, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this."

I shall now explain for you the temporal limits and stages of the fulfillment of faith. Good son, all practitioners proceed from the stage of being bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) into the stage of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).

After ten thousand three thousand kalpas have passed, they immediately achieve the ten kinds of faith and enter the Bodhisattva’s first dwelling, the Stage of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*). Second, they gather immeasurable...

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (The Stages of Yoga Practice): Furthermore, a "Bodhisattva by designation" (*prajñapti-bodhisattva*) on the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), having completed a duration of sixty-four thousand *kalpas*, immediately achieves the ten kinds of joyful mind and attains the adamantine stage (*vajra-bhūmi*).

According to the *Tri-sarvajñatā-prakaraṇa-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Dhāraṇī of the Threefold Wisdom): Beings of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) mostly pass through eighty-one thousand five hundred *kalpas*.
It is already completed. Having accomplished faith, one is certain not to regress. The *Sūtra on the Names of the Four Dharma-Gates* states:
"Furthermore, when an ordinary person at the stage of aspiring faith has passed twenty-six thousand kalpas, their faith will be fully accomplished without any deficiency.
The *Sūtra on the Five Pure Samādhis* states: "If there are sentient beings who enter..."

Regarding the practice of faith on the Ground of Difficult Angles (*Durgāṅga-bhūmi*), once ninety thousand *kalpas* have been fully completed, the stage of the "Perfection of Faith" (*śraddhā-pariniṣpatti*) is achieved.
The *Sūtra of the Six Vajra Dhāraṇīs* states: "The measure of the perfection of faith is forty-eight thousand and sixty *kalpas*.
The *Sūtra of the Great Wisdom Radiance* states: "Furthermore, son of good family, if there are sentient beings..."
When one is born as a parent of the roots of goodness and merit that seek accomplishment—acting as the earth and heaven—one must pass through the duration of ten *kṣaṇas*.
Once this is completed, the ground of faith becomes level and free of weeds. As the *Sūtra on the Determination of the Ultimate Limit of the Eight Real Phases* states:
"When the stage of faith is accomplished, within the very first *kṣaṇa* in which the mind of faith arises, the ten kinds of faith are present."
It is fully perfected. The *Mañjuśrī-paripūrṇa-hetu-sāgara-mahā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states:
"Once three asaṃkhyeya great immeasurable kalpas have passed, the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi) is then fully established.
The *Gambhīra-bodhi-hetupratyaya-sūtra* states: "The establishment of the stage of faith takes only thirty thousand kalpas."
The *Sūtra on the Skillful Expedient Wisdom of the Eleven Great Ones* states:
"A Bodhisattva practicing through faith will, after a period of nine thousand kalpas, definitely achieve pure faith and contemplate the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The *Sūtra on the Universal Illumination of the Bodhisattvas' Radiance* states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajramati addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One...'"
“World-Honored One, how much time must pass for the initial seed-ground of unsurpassed bodhi to reach definitive maturity, so that the sprout of bodhi may emerge and grow?
The Buddha said: “To accomplish the initial seed-ground, one must pass through seventy-five thousand and sixty kalpas.
Once the initial seed-ground is fully established, there are thirteen stages of receiving predictions.”
The *Samayika-sūtra* states: "The accomplishment of faith is neither distant nor near; neither non-existent nor existent; neither high nor low; neither beginning nor end;
neither departing nor arriving; neither great nor small; neither belonging to the three periods of time nor not belonging to the three periods of time;
neither a stage nor a ground; neither good nor evil; neither right nor wrong. It transcends the path of language and the mind..."
When the sphere of activity ceases, it is therefore called the stage of true faith. The *Tathāgatagarbha-mūlavijñāna-sūtra* states:
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what is meant by the 'Stage of Faith' which is the ground of vast and perfect merit and virtue? The Buddha said: "The ten faiths and the ten..."

Faith. The ten understandings (daśa-vijñapti) and the ten faiths; the ten practices (daśa-caryā) and the ten faiths; the ten transferences (daśa-pratipatti) and the ten faiths; the ten stages (daśa-bhūmi) and the ten faiths; the Buddha-stage and the ten faiths;
even down to the stage of those with full fetters and evil seeds, as well as all practitioners of the two vehicles—all possess these ten faiths.
All phenomena, immeasurable and boundless, are such that there is not a single dharma that is not comprised within the ten faiths.
For this reason, it is called the "vast and perfect stage of faith. The *Bodhisattva-avataṃsaka-mūla-karma-sūtra* states:
"The Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa practiced the ten precepts for ten thousand kalpas, establishing them with certainty; thus, his faith was perfected."
Regarding the locus: for what reason do these various sūtras exhibit such distinctions? It is because the minds of sentient beings are immeasurable and boundless, each being distinct;
according to their respective mental states (*citta-prakāra*), the characteristics of faith and practice are taught, and thus they differ in this way.
One should examine and deliberate upon this carefully. For the time being, this passage provides an explanation based solely on the *Mūla-karmas*.
The root text states: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct one to resolve to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Alternatively, one may resolve to attain enlightenment out of great compassion;
or, when the True Dharma is about to perish, one may resolve to attain enlightenment through the causal conditions of protecting the Dharma."
The Commentary says: This reveals the gateway of the causes and conditions for generating the resolve [for awakening].
That is to say, for a practitioner who has already achieved faith, in order to give rise to the mind of the first stage (*vihāra*), one must generate it by depending on the power of conditions.
Within this passage, there are three types: first, the cause and condition of requesting [the Buddhas], namely, all the infinite and boundless Buddhas.
Together with the assembly of great bodhisattvas, they manifest an ocean of various supreme and wondrous teachings and sūtras.

Practitioners at the stage of faith offer exhortations and requests for instruction so that they may transcend the stage of uncertainty, become firmly established, and abide in the realm of immovability.
Second is the causal condition of deliverance, which refers to [the compassion] directed toward the ocean of all sufferings of immeasurable and boundless sentient beings.
Taking this as the cause, one gives rise to the vast, pure, and non-retrogressive great mind of compassion that is adamantine.

Third, the causal conditions for protecting the Dharma: when the Buddha’s teachings are about to perish, one employs various skillful means—according to what is appropriate, suitable, and timely—to protect the Buddha-Dharma at all times and in all places, without sparing even one's own body or life.
It should be understood as follows: by the power of great causal conditions, one is able to personally initiate the vast, pure, and long-enduring mind of the non-regressive vajra.
The text states: "Those who, having thus perfected their faith, give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, enter the stage of right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) and never again regress.
This is called abiding within the lineage of the Tathāgata, in accord with the primary cause."

The treatise says: This demonstrates the superior gateway of the stage of attaining benefit. That is to say, one who has accomplished faith and attained the practice of liberation possesses ten names because they are free from regression.

First, they are called "one free from sorrow and affliction," because they have distanced themselves from the fear of the mind that regresses and falls into the ground of afflictions belonging to ordinary beings. Second, they are called "a person of great wealth and nobility."
First, they are called those who have cleared away the wilderness and filth of afflictions (*kleśa*), for they gather and preserve the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.

Second, they are called those of noble and superior lineage, for they have distanced themselves from the inferior lineage of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and have entered the exalted lineage of the Tathāgatas.
Third, they are called those with complete hands and feet, for they grasp the torch of Prajñā and traverse the vastness of the *dharmadhātu*.
Fifth, they are called those who create the great river of water, for they flow directly and unimpededly into the great ocean of *sārvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Sixth, they are called those who establish a palace, for they have already transcended the indeterminate and dwell securely within the household of the Tathāgata.
Seventh, they are called true sons of the Buddha, for they have distanced themselves from the ordinary womb.

1. Because they have entered the noble womb (*āryagarbha*). 2. They are called persons who are great fields of merit (*mahāpuṇyakṣetra*), because they have emerged from afflictions and are uniquely pure.
3. They are called persons with immeasurable retinues, because all sentient beings of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are taken as their own kin.
4. They are called persons without obstruction, because they act in accordance with the turning of the mind.

The text states: "If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are meager and whose afflictions have been deep-seated for a long time, although they may encounter a Buddha and even make offerings to him, they will only give rise to the seeds of humans and devas, or the seeds of the two vehicles."
The Commentary states: This is the "Gate of Manifesting the Superior by Citing the Inferior," which gives rise to understanding. Within this gate, there are two sub-gates:
first, the "Gate of Manifesting the Inferior Characteristics by Citing the Inferior"; second, the "Gate of Manifesting the Superior Characteristics by Citing the Superior. This is the former gate.
This refers to ordinary beings whose roots of goodness are feeble and whose afflictions are deep-seated;
although they encounter the conditions for the Mahāyāna, they give rise to the seeds of only minor roots of goodness.
The *Ben* (Root) says: "Suppose there are those who seek the Mahāyāna, yet their faculties (*indriya*) are not fixed;
they may advance or retreat. The *Lun* (Commentary) says: This is the "Gate of Revealing the Superior Form" by citing the superior [case].

That is to say, if there are sentient beings who seek the profound and subtle Dharma-gate of the Mahāyāna, their minds immediately become unable to reach a state of certainty. Even when encountering favorable conditions...
Vaguely and suddenly, as if advancing, one encounters adverse conditions and naturally retreats; this is because the mind lacks stability.
If one cannot achieve stability, how can they be called a superior person? Although they lack stability, the Dharma they aspire to is extremely superior and sublime.
Furthermore, it is because they give rise to the seeds for the two vehicles of humans and devas.

The *Ben* (Root Text) says: "There are some who make offerings to the Buddhas; even before ten thousand kalpas have passed, they may encounter conditions therein and likewise give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
The *Lun* (Commentary) says: "This demonstrates that there is no fixed time for the accomplishment of faith, thereby explaining the great meaning of the fourteenth sutra."
Consider this: it is said that if there are sentient beings who make offerings to the Buddhas and achieve faith, the timing of this is not fixed;
it may be extremely distant, extremely near, or somewhere in between. Why is this? Because faith arises as it ripens, according to the presence or absence of conditions.
The text states: "That is to say, one may resolve their mind upon seeing the physical marks and features of a Buddha; or they may resolve their mind by making offerings to sentient beings;
or they may resolve their mind through the instruction of those of the Two Vehicles; or they may resolve their mind by emulating others."
The Commentary states: This distinct explanation of "formative activity" (*abhisamskāra*) reveals the characteristics of the causes and conditions for generating the resolve [for awakening].
Within this text, there are four kinds of causes and conditions for generating the resolve: first, the cause and condition of seeing the Buddha;
because by seeing the Tathāgata’s body of wondrous form, one is able to generate the vast mind. Second, the cause and condition of making offerings to the Saṃgha; because by planting...
First, the causal condition of providing various offerings to the Saṃgha; because through these causes and conditions one is able to give rise to a vast mind.

Second, the causal condition of shame and remorse; seeing and hearing the teachings of those of the Two Vehicles, one feels shame and remorse for their inferiority, and through these causes and conditions one is able to give rise to a vast mind.
Third, the causal condition of following and assisting others; by following the altruistic intentions of others...
It is because through these causes and conditions one is able to give rise to the vast mind.

The original text says: "The arousal of the mind in such ways as these is entirely indeterminate; encountering adverse causes and conditions, it may suddenly be lost and one falls to the level of the two vehicles."

The Commentary states: This serves as the causal condition to reveal the characteristics of the ten types of indeterminate faith within the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra*), and to provide a summary conclusion for the previously explained section on the determination of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā-viniścaya*).

For what reason are these ten categories of faith designated as "indeterminate"? It is because if one encounters favorable conditions, one proceeds toward the higher realms; however, if one meets with...
Due to the causes and conditions of opposition and transgression, one should proceed toward the evil realms; it is like light feathers that, being blown by the wind, turn hither and thither.
Having explained the first set of two gates, I shall now explain the second set of two gates.

The Text says: "Furthermore, regarding the 'arousing of the mind through the perfection of faith,' what kind of mind is aroused? Briefly stated, there are three kinds. What are these three? The Commentary says:
"Regarding 'what kind of mind is aroused,' this is the introductory section that opens the inquiry and provides a general outline. That is to say, it initiates the opening..."
The question, "In brief, there are three kinds," is a general summary and a general answer because it serves as a general inquiry.
The phrase, "What are the three? is a general enumeration and a general question.

The text states: First is the direct mind, because it maintains right mindfulness of the dharma of True Suchness. Second is the profound mind, because it delights in accumulating all various virtuous practices.
Third is the mind of great compassion, because it desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings.

The treatise says: This directly clarifies the gate of answering and explaining through extensive exposition. Within this, there are three parts. Among these three, the first pertains to both self-benefit and benefit for others;

the middle pertains only to self-benefit; and the last pertains only to benefit for others. Furthermore, the first two belong exclusively to the category of self-benefit, while the last one is for the benefit of others.
Furthermore, since all three pertain to both, [they constitute] the first: the gate of skillful means for right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
First is the gate of the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*), which serves as the skillful means for the wisdom of the true essence (*tattva-jñāna*).
Second is the gate of the fulfillment of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*), which serves as the skillful means for abiding in all virtues by means of the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*).

Third is the gate of the accomplishment of peace and happiness (*sukha-siddhi*), which refers to the compassionate mind (*karuṇā-citta*) that is able to effectively rescue and deliver all sentient beings from immeasurable suffering and affliction, causing them to attain vast and great security.
Because of delight [in practice].

The original text says: Question: Since it was previously taught that the Dharma-realm has a single characteristic and the Buddha-body is non-dual, why is one not simply mindful of True Suchness (tathatā), but instead relies on seeking and practicing various wholesome deeds?
The Commentary states: This explains the "Gate of Questioning and Answering to Resolve Doubts. This gate has two parts:
first, the "Gate of Difficult Questions Regarding Contradictions Between Precedent and Subsequent [Passages]"; second, the "Gate of Opening, Clarifying, and Explaining to Dissolve Difficulties.

This is the first gate, which means raising two preceding and succeeding passages that appear contradictory in order to question their distinct characteristics. How are they contradictory? It refers to the preceding passage...
It is stated as follows: "The meaning of 'enlightenment' (bodhi) refers to the essence of mind being free from the marks of thought.

This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception. The single mark of the Dharma-realm is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body.
Based upon this Dharma-body, it is termed 'Original Enlightenment' (mūla-bodhi). In the subsequent text, it is stated as follows: "Secondly..."
Because the profound mind delights in accumulating all virtuous practices, the preceding and succeeding passages appear contradictory;
therefore, a question is raised. This is the interrogative statement, which challenges their differing characteristics and should be carefully examined and discerned.
The text says: The answer is as follows. For example, the nature of a great maṇi jewel is luminous and pure, yet it is defiled by the impurities of ore.
Even if a person contemplates the quality of the jewel’s nature, if they do not employ various skillful means to grind and polish it, it will never become pure.

The Treatise says: This is the section on "Opening the Way, Synthesizing Explanations, and Resolving Difficulties. Within this, there are seven parts: first, the section on directly answering and decisively resolving those difficulties;
second, the section on the benefits gained by those who practice wholesome deeds; third, the section on the skillful means of cultivation.
1. The section on revealing the merits of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*); 2. The section on distinguishing the superior and inferior to reveal their differences;

3. The section on resolving doubts through the texts of the *sūtras*; 4. The section on praising the merits of generating the resolve. The first section has three parts: 1. The section on skillfully presenting analogies; 2.
The section on establishing the correspondence through combined exposition; 3. The section on revealing the teaching by way of the Dharma.
The Gateway of Arising Understanding. This is the first gateway. Within it, there are four parts. First, the analogy of the jewel: namely, the great maṇi-jewel.
Where would such a jewel be found? Such a jewel would be found in yellow stone. What is its color? It is a deep yellow. What is the shape of its body like?
That is to say, they are arranged like squares because they have no length or shortness. As for the dimensions of these large and small forms, it is said they are one *zhang* [ten feet] each.
Thus, among all the yellow stones, every one is fully endowed with jewels; there is no yellow stone that lacks a *maṇi*.
As for the sequence of their arrangement: first is the jewel, second is the gold, and third...
Third, regarding the substance of the stone: among these yellow stones, some are extremely small while others are extremely large, each being distinct.
How could it be said that they all pervade everything? This *maṇi* jewel possesses a preeminent power;
although it is only one *vyāma* in size, it pervades the large, the medium, and the small without exception, leaving nothing uncovered.
Regarding obstructions: it may also be said that they pervade all places, because this jewel exists within that stone;
one should carefully observe that the color of the stone is yellow. Second, the analogy of natural purity:
such a jewel is extremely clear in its essential nature because it is free from the accumulation of dust; it is like the original nature being clear and bright. Third, the analogy of defilement.
In this way, a jewel may be obstructed by gold ore, stone, and the like, such that its bright and pure characteristics cannot manifest;

it remains as it was, possessing the impurities of mineral dross. The analogy of the four groups of people refers to those who are utterly impoverished and extremely indolent, and those who do not seek the jewel, as well as those who are diligent and delight in seeking the jewel. As the original text states: "If..."

Although people contemplate the nature of jewels and so forth, having already explained the gate of skillful means through the presentation of metaphors, we shall now explain the gate of establishing the correspondence through application.
Within the metaphor of the jewels, the term "great maṇi jewel" should be understood as a metaphor for the originally awakened buddha-nature (*prakṛti-āśraya-buddhadhātu*). Why is this so?
The originally enlightened Buddha-nature is hidden within the continuum of the bodies of sentient beings; it is like that jewel.
The mention of "yellow stone" serves as a metaphor for the continuum of the bodies of all sentient beings. Why is this so?

Because the Buddha-nature is concealed and wrapped within the bodies of all sentient beings, it is like that stone. The mention of its "yellow color" serves as a metaphor for that Buddha-nature, which is unchanging.
This is because of its meaning. Why is this so? Because *tathatā* (suchness) and Buddha-nature are firm and unchanging, they resemble that gold.
As for the statement that "sitting upright is neither long nor short," it serves as a metaphor for the equality of the *tathatā*-dharma, which has neither increase nor decrease.
Why is this so? Because this *tathatā*-dharma is of a single flavor and equal, without any differentiation; it resembles that sitting posture.
The mention of "one zhang" (a measure of length) serves as a metaphor for the True Suchness (*tathatā*) being fully complete and perfect, without any deficiency.
Why is this so? Because the Dharma-body of True Suchness is endowed with the ten thousand virtues and lacks nothing; it resembles that *zhang* in this regard.

The statement that "such jewel-treasures are found within all yellow stones, and there is no yellow stone that does not contain them" means that they are entirely present within them. There is no yellow stone that is devoid of the *maṇi*.
The "noble woman" (ni) should be understood as an analogy for the nature of True Suchness (tathatā), which pervades the various bodies of all sentient beings;

for there is no sentient being who lacks the fundamental awakening of the nature of True Suchness. Why is this so? Because this nature of True Suchness is free from non-pervasiveness, resembling that jewel.
As for the mention of the first jewel, the second gold, and the third stone substance, it should be understood as follows:
This serves as an analogy for the sequential dharmas that coexist [with the source], because they gradually manifest with increasing coarseness. Why is this so?

When the ocean of the four marks (lakṣaṇa) is established through the flow from original enlightenment-wisdom (mūla-awakening), they gradually manifest with increasing coarseness according to their respective order, resembling those three [marks].
It is said that this mani-jewel possesses a sublime power; although it is only one *vyāma* in size, it pervades the large, the medium, and the small.

The phrase "without exception within" should be understood as an analogy for the inconceivable activity of the fundamental awakening of *tathatā*, which pervades the bodies of all beings—whether small like mosquitoes or large like dragons—without any hindrance or difficulty. Why is this so?
Because the nature of this *tathatā*-dharma is equal and pervasive throughout both ordinary beings and sages, resembling that jewel; it is said that this treasure exists within those stones. Its...

The yellow color of the stone should be understood as a metaphor for the fact that all sentient beings possess fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), because they possess the characteristics of mind.
Why is this so? Because all sentient beings possess an awakened mind and have the consciousness of discernment (*vijñāna*); in this respect, they resemble that stone.
Next is the section on the "Door of Concordant Application" which explains the analogy of purity: it is said that the substance and nature of such a jewel are exceedingly luminous.

The statement "white and far removed from dust and entanglements" should be understood as a metaphor for the intrinsically pure fundamental awakening (*prakṛti-viśuddha-mūla-bodhi*), which is clear, bright, and free from defilement.
Next is the section on the "Gate of Concordant Application," which explains the metaphors for defilement and their correspondence.

It says that although such a jewel can be obstructed by gold, stone, and the like, preventing its bright appearance from manifesting, this should be understood as a metaphor for the self-nature pure mind (*svabhāva-viśuddha-citta*).
Because it is obscured and covered by ignorance, the untainted nature-virtue cannot manifest; therefore, next is explained the "Gate of Concordant Application through the Analogy of Humans.

Regarding the two types of people: they correspond to the analogy of one who seeks the treasure of the Buddha-dharma with extreme diligence and one who is extremely indolent, as stated in the original text: "Such sentient beings."
The text states: "The dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) is empty and pure in its essential nature, yet it possesses immeasurable defilements of affliction.
Even if a person contemplates True Suchness, they will not attain purity without employing various skillful means for repeated cultivation.
Because these defilements are immeasurable and pervade all wholesome dharmas, one must cultivate all virtuous practices as an antidote."

The Commentary states: This demonstrates the gateway of generating understanding through the teaching of the Dharma. Herein, according to their respective order, the application of the Dharma to the simile generates understanding in the practitioner;
this should be carefully examined and discerned. Since the meaning of the text is clear, there is no need for a separate explanation.
The Text says: "If a person practices all wholesome dharmas, they naturally accord with and conform to the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā).
The Commentary says: This is the gate of benefiting for those who practice wholesome deeds.

That is to say, if there are sentient beings who sever all evils and cultivate all virtues, they will naturally and spontaneously obtain the pearl of True Suchness, which illuminates and penetrates the dark night of ignorance.
Because there is no doubt or fear. The Root Text says:
"Briefly stated, there are four kinds of skillful means (*upāya*). What are the four? The Commentary says:
"This is the gateway of skillful means for this practice. This gateway has four [parts]: first, all cultivation..."
1. The gateway of practicing the fundamental [practices]; 2. The gateway of subduing evil karma so that it does not arise; 3. The gateway of generating and increasing roots of goodness;
4. The gateway of boundless and impartial vows.

The text says: First is the fundamental expedient of practice. This means contemplating that all phenomena (dharmas) are devoid of intrinsic nature and free from deluded views, thereby not abiding in saṃsāra.
It means contemplating that all phenomena arise from the harmony of causes and conditions, wherein roots and fruits are never lost;

thus, one gives rise to great compassion, cultivates various merits, and gathers and transforms sentient beings, yet does not abide in nirvāṇa. This is because it accords with the nature of reality (dharmatā).
Because it abides.

The treatise says: Within this first gate, there are two parts. First is the gate of the accomplishment of non-abiding prajñā, which is to observe that all phenomena are from the very beginning unborn and unceasing, ultimately quiescent, and entirely...
There is nothing that exists, because one does not abide in saṃsāra. Second is the accomplishment of the gate of non-abiding through great compassion.
This refers to the observation that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; thus, cause and effect are not empty, and karmic retribution likewise exists.
Taking the ocean of the realms of infinite and boundless sentient beings as the ultimate object of grasping, one does not abide in nirvāṇa.

Regarding the phrase "because it accords with the non-abiding nature of reality (*dharmatā*)," this demonstrates both the conditions and the conclusion of the two types of practice regarding the path of non-abiding.
Although the dharma-gates of cultivation are immeasurable, the path of non-abiding is their most fundamental root;
therefore, it is said to be the "fundamental skillful means (*upāya*) of practice."
The root text says: Second is the skillful means of cessation, which refers to shame, remorse, and repentance.
These are able to cease all unwholesome dharmas so that they do not increase, because by conforming to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one becomes free from all faults.
The Commentary says: This is the gateway for subduing evil karma so that it does not arise.

This gateway is intended to demonstrate that the practitioner should give rise to pure mental states such as shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), thereby preventing all immeasurable misdeeds and gradually diminishing them so they do not increase.
The phrase "because it accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and is free from all faults" serves as the summary.
Regarding the conditions for this:
the root text states, "Third is the skillful means for initiating and increasing roots of goodness. This refers to diligently making offerings and prostrating to the Triple Gem;
praising, rejoicing in, and requesting the Buddhas. Because of a heart of pure devotion and reverence for the Triple Gem, one's faith increases."

Excellent! You are thus able to resolve to seek the unsurpassed path. Furthermore, because you are protected by the power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, you are able to eliminate karmic obstructions and ensure that your roots of goodness do not regress;
for by conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), you have become free from the obstruction of delusion.
The Commentary says: This is the gateway for the arising and growth of roots of goodness.
This gateway is intended to demonstrate that the practitioner should, with respect to all Three Jewels, perform acts of reverence, offering, prostration, praise, sympathetic joy, and entreaty;
thereby increasing their faith, eliminating karmic obstructions, and aspiring to the unsurpassed Great Bodhi, in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"Because of being free from the obstacle of delusion" summarizes its conditions.
The original text states: "The fourth is the skillful means of great vows that are impartial.

This refers to making the vow to continue until the end of the future, to transform and deliver all sentient beings without exception, causing them all to ultimately attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder, in accordance with the Dharma."
Because its nature is without interruption.

The treatise says: This is the gate of boundless equality of the vow. This gate is intended to reveal that the practitioner should give rise to vast vows as numerous as the atoms of the worlds of the ten directions, and cultivate the ocean [of merit] throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
The ocean of causal practices, as numerous as the atoms within the realms, gathers in oceans of sentient beings as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions,
and brings to fulfillment oceans of resultant perfections as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions; because all of these are without exception,
and because they accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without interruption, this summarizes their conditions.
The text states: "The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is vast and great, pervading all sentient beings; it is equal and non-dual, without thoughts of self or other, for it is ultimately quiescent."
The Commentary says: This is a manifestation of the characteristics that accord with excellence. For what reason?

Because within the four concluding sections, they are all collectively termed "accordant with the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*). This is intended to manifest that the nature of phenomena is like space;
its essential substance is vast, perfect, and without limit; its characteristics and functions are unimpeded and sovereign, and it has no beginning.

End. It is likewise for all practitioners who cultivate those four gates; they proceed in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*), because their *āśaya* (resolute intention) is vast, perfect, and without limit.
The text states: Because the Bodhisattva has given rise to this mind, he attains a partial vision of the Dharmakāya.

By virtue of seeing the Dharmakāya, according to his power of aspiration, he is able to manifest eight kinds of manifestations for the benefit of sentient beings, namely: descending from Tuṣita Heaven;
Entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, and emerging from the womb; leaving the household life, attaining the Way, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering nirvana.
The Commentary says: This is the gateway for manifesting the merit of generating the bodhicitta.

This passage is intended to manifest that a Bodhisattva dwelling in the initial generation of the mind gives rise to a vast and perfect mind that accords with the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; it is a wisdom of concordant contemplation.
One perceives the Dharma-nature body. Because one perceives the Dharma-nature body, there is mastery over the power of vows.
By virtue of this power of vows, one gives rise to great compassion toward sentient beings throughout the immeasurable and boundless realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Because this great compassion is exceedingly profound, eight kinds of manifestations for peaceful and blissful transformation appear—according to the time, the place, the suitability, and the response—in accordance with [the needs of beings].
It accords with suchness (*tathatā*) because it brings about benefit, peace, and happiness.

The original text states: "However, this Bodhisattva is not yet called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), because since immeasurable past eons, their out-flowing karma (*sāsrava-karman*) has not been definitively severed;
thus, wherever they are born, they remain associated with subtle suffering. Furthermore, they are not bound by karma."
Because they possess the sovereign power of great vows. The treatise says:

This section distinguishes the superior and inferior by clarifying the different categories (*viśeṣa-mukha*). Within this, there are two parts. First, the category distinguishing [the initial stage] from the stages above the ground (*bhūmi*).
That is to say, a Bodhisattva in the Stage of Resolving the Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*) is only called a body of illusory transformation and reflection; it cannot be called "real."
This is because they are like Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body. Why is this so? Because these Bodhisattvas have not yet emerged from the residual karma of beginningless time;
wherever they take birth, they remain inseparable from subtle suffering. This is contrary to the case of Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), who possess the opposite characteristics.

This statement serves to distinguish them from those still bound by fetters (*paryavasthāna*); that is to say, the Bodhisattva in the stage of the Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*) is unconditioned.
The characteristic of the causal aspect of karma that functions in conjunction with bondage is the absence of the fruit of rebirth resulting from fetters. Why is this?
Because it functions through the fulfillment of great vows and skillful means.
The text states: "As it is said in the sūtras, there are those who fall back and descend into the evil realms; this is not an actual falling back.
It is merely for the sake of inspiring diligence and courage in beginner bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the stage of certainty and might otherwise become indolent."
The Commentary states: This treatise is a section for resolving doubts based on the texts of the *Sūtras*.
There are five types of such [sūtra] citations. First, it is said in the *Mañjuśrī-pramuditā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*:
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, you have always proclaimed these words within the great assembly: 'The fifty seed-syllables are the adornment...'"
The ocean-like practice of the fruit of discipline is the foundation of all causal practices; all practitioners must traverse this path to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.
Within these fifty seed-minds, how many belong to the category of retrogression and how many belong to the category of stability?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me. Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "Listen attentively..."
Listen attentively. Reflect upon it well. I shall now explain it to you in detail for your sake.
Noble son, the ten stages of reality (*bhūmi*) are called the stage of the adamantine *prajñā*.
The preceding forty mental states are called the stage of the crystal-bead-like turning-and-transforming dedication. You should know it thus; you should contemplate it thus. Now, in this sutra...
The text is intended to reveal the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Great Being (*mahāsattva*). That which has already been truly realized is called the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhāga*);
because the forty types of mind prior to this have not yet attained realization, they are called the stage of retrogression (*parihāṇa-bhāga*).

Second, according to the *Sūtra on the Spontaneous Infusion of Innate Awakening and Great Compassion*, it says: "Furthermore, Son of the Buddha, as to what you previously asked: 'What is meant by...'"
Regarding the "signs of regression," this matter is supreme and inconceivable among the inconceivable;
it is beyond the comprehension of foolish ordinary beings and bodhisattvas who have only recently resolved their minds.
