They manifest in all manner of diverse forms and come to where the practitioner is, disturbing the practitioner’s mind.
At that time, one should each recite the following mantra. This divine mantra is universal and not specific;
it is the great *dhāraṇī* spoken in the *Tathāgata-dharmakośa-hetupratyaya-sūtra*. As that sutra says:

At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, when all manner of followers of heterodox paths come to where the practitioner dwells and disturb the practitioner’s mind, by what gate should they be expelled?
Thereupon, the Tathāgata told Mañjuśrī: “There is a profound Dharma-gate that can skillfully [expel them].”

This universally cures all heterodox paths; it is the Great Dharani Dharma-gate of the Totality of Mantras, which accords with and follows the transformations of the *Indra-jāla* net, the unimpeded and sovereign seal of the inexhaustible treasury of all Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you, Mañjuśrī.

That which is called the Dharma-gate of the Great Dhāraṇī of Unobstructed Mastery and Thorough Penetration is the precious treasury protected and remembered by all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time;

it is the great rule constantly recited and maintained by all Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and three periods of time; and it is [the teaching] of all divine kings and spirits of the ten directions and three periods of time...
All devas and humans alike should pay homage to and make offerings to this vast field of merit.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One recited the mantra: *Tadyathā | Naraśigano udiccha maṇḍa | Svati āhaṇi*.
Dhāni. Bhagavati dṛḍha u-mari-jaṇa-vani-te. Kātan śiva-yata. Kauṭi-na-pati-sabhā-i. Vata-ni-vi. Svāhā.
Ukkatthāṇivī. Caṭṭakhāye. Kanna-sisā svāhā.
If this divine mantra has been recited eight thousand seven hundred and fifty-one times, all classes of malevolent beings will accordingly be driven away and defeated;
they shall no longer be able to cause affliction or disturbance.
The text states: "Sometimes he speaks of dhāraṇīs; sometimes he speaks of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;

or he speaks of equality, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, absence of enmity, absence of kinship, absence of cause, and absence of effect—ultimate emptiness and stillness, which is true nirvāṇa."

The treatise says: This explains the gate of the deluded consciousness that manifests through verbal expression. This gate has three aspects: first, the teaching on the *dhāraṇī* gate; second, the teaching on the gate of the causes for practice;
and third, the teaching on the gate of the virtues of perfected fruition. Regarding these three teachings, who is it that speaks each?
Specifically, when appearing in the form of a deva, one primarily teaches the *dhāraṇī*; when appearing in the form of a bodhisattva, one primarily teaches...
This is the causal practice. If the image of the Tathāgata speaks extensively of the qualities of the fruit, why is this?
It is because each speaks according to what they themselves have realized, so that practitioners may develop faith. As for the dhāraṇī that is spoken, what are its characteristics?
It is called the "Dhāraṇī of Continuous Radiance. Therefore, if one recites this mantra, what benefit will there be? That is to say, if one recites this—
Mantra. Because the radiance of one’s own body continues into the bodies of others, the celestial image comes to the place where that practitioner resides.
Having spoken this *dhāraṇī* gateway, the practitioner—who previously lacked radiance—now possesses radiance;
because of this extreme joy, they form this thought: "It is now by virtue of the power of my practice..."
Now, there is such a sublime radiance that disturbs one’s own correct practice and causes one to enter the net of external heterodoxy.
For this reason, that celestial image spoke a gateway of dhāraṇī, reciting the mantra as follows:
Aṅgāṅga mā mā apavi. Nakhe. Upasaṇidikhaye. Āhate te te paviha. Vana-kūvate kama-le. Kṣaṃtani-ta-ta-tani. Svāhā svāhā svāhā. A.
*Tāni tāni svāhā*. When this divine mantra has been recited five thousand three hundred times, a continuous stream of light will immediately form a single [mass].
At that time, the practitioner shall recite the mantra, saying:
Tadyathā maṇi apadāte khabhaṇani yamodite.
Bakhanaradevīhotebabhanadi. Tavadāma rāsa svāhā.
If this divine mantra is recited one hundred times, the radiance of that body will be severed and no longer cling to it; ultimately, it shall not [be affected by...].

[This is] vexation. Next, the gate of the causes for practicing cultivation is explained. Although there are immeasurable gates for the causes of practicing cultivation, they do not exceed the six *pāramitās*.
Therefore, those [adversaries] speak of six provisions (*sambhāra*) to practitioners, thereby confusing those practitioners and causing them to enter the net of error.
What benefit can such non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) possibly have? They speak thus to cause confusion.
The practitioner is mistaken. At that time, the practitioner’s intention was to sever all evil, cultivate all goodness, and perfect the causal practices without any deficiency.
That non-Buddhist teacher manifested himself as being of like mind, causing [the practitioner] to abandon the right path and turn toward a wrong path;
therefore, he taught the six perfections. Next, he taught the gateway of the virtues of the perfected fruit, which is the perfection of the result.
Although there are immeasurable gateways, they do not transcend the realm of tranquil nirvāṇa.
Therefore, those images speak of the virtues of nirvāṇa to the practitioner, yet they distract that practitioner and cause them to enter the net of error.
What benefit could such non-Buddhist practitioners possibly have? They speak in this way to mislead the practitioner. That practitioner, by virtue of that intention, [is led astray].
Because it is for the sake of realizing the fruit [of enlightenment], this is why external paths manifest the superior fruits and virtues that practitioners seek to attain.
The minds of those practitioners become attached to them, causing them to incline toward false paths. As stated in the original text, they may speak of "equality," "emptiness," and so forth.
The *Ben* (Main Text) says: "Or they cause others to know past events from former lives, and they also know future events, attaining the knowledge of others' minds.
The *Lun* (Commentary) says:
"This explains the gateway for deluding people by attaining knowledge of the three periods of time. Such is the respective characteristic of these three types of penetrating knowledge (*trividyā*)."
How is this so? It means that the two types of penetrating knowledge regarding the past and the future each penetrate their respective objects.
Regarding the most distant limit, it extends to eighty thousand kalpas; regarding the most proximate limit, it can thoroughly penetrate events of a single lifetime.

As for what is called "penetrating knowledge of the present," this is precisely the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), because it is able to penetrate the various minds of present persons.
As it was originally attained through the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
The original text says: "Unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*) can cause sentient beings to become greedily attached to worldly matters of fame and profit.

The commentary says: This establishes the gate of not being separated from the fetters and entanglements of the world; that is to say, it causes those who follow external paths (*tīrthika*) to achieve [such attachments].
There are one hundred and forty-six thousand varieties of worldly treatises and one hundred and eight thousand varieties of skill in frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Because these bind and entangle sentient beings, causing them to remain in the world and fail to achieve liberation.
The text states: Furthermore, it causes those sent as messengers to frequently become angry and frequently joyful, their natures lacking constancy.

They may become excessively compassionate, excessively drowsy, or frequently ill; their minds may become indolent, or they may suddenly exert diligence only to later abandon it. They may give rise to lack of faith, becoming full of doubt and excessive deliberation;
or they may abandon their original superior practices to cultivate miscellaneous activities, or become attached to worldly affairs, entangled by various distractions.
The treatise states: This explains the gateway of the mind’s nature being impermanent and giving rise to confusion.

That is to say, it destroys firm faith and causes the mind to conceive of impermanence; it severs the feet of practice and blocks the path of entry, leading one into the net of error and into the state of non-nature.
The text states: "It can also cause people to attain various samādhis that are merely partial resemblances; these are all attained by non-Buddhists and are not true samādhi.

Or it may cause people to abide in meditative concentration for one day, two days, three days, or even up to seven days, obtaining naturally fragrant and delicious food and drink, with body and mind feeling at ease and contented, neither hungry nor thirsty."
It causes people to become attached; it may also cause people to eat without moderation, sometimes too much and sometimes too little, so that their complexion changes.
The commentary states: This explains how one attains false concentration rather than the true gateway.
That is to say, non-Buddhist practitioners attain twenty-one kinds of false samādhis, which disturb those who practice and cause them to enter the net of falsehood.
The text says: For this reason, the practitioner should constantly observe with wisdom so that this mind does not follow the net of the heterodox.
One should diligently maintain right mindfulness, neither grasping nor clinging; thus one will be able to remain far removed from all these karmic obstructions.
The Commentary states: This explains that it exhorts the practitioner to depart from false paths and encourages the cultivation of wisdom;
through various skillful discernments, it removes the disease of ignorance and dispels the errors of heterodox doctrines.

The text states: "One should know that all samādhis of the non-Buddhists do not depart from the mind of views, craving, and self-conceit, because they are greedily attached to worldly fame, profit, and honor.
As for the samādhi of True Suchness (tathatā), one does not dwell on the mark of seeing, nor does one dwell on the mark of attainment;
even upon emerging from meditative concentration, there is no indolence or arrogance. All afflictions gradually become thin and subtle. If ordinary people..."
It is impossible for one who has not practiced this samādhi-dharma to enter the lineage of the Tathāgatas.

This is because those who cultivate worldly meditative absorptions (dhyāna-samādhi) frequently give rise to attachment to their flavors; relying on the view of self (ātman-dṛṣṭi), they remain bound to the three realms and share commonality with non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
Furthermore, if they are not protected by a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they will give rise to the views of non-Buddhists.
The Commentary says: This explains the gate for discerning the true from the false so as to bring about clear understanding.
That which accords with the mundane world is called a "false samādhi," while that which accords with the supramundane world is called a "true samādhi.
These two kinds of samādhi should be understood in this way.
The Text says: "Furthermore, those who diligently and single-mindedly practice and study this samādhi shall obtain ten kinds of benefits in the present life.

The Commentary says: This is the section praising the merits of the samādhi, which consists of two parts: first, the section providing a general outline; second, [the section providing detailed explanation].
The Section on Detailed Exposition. This section serves as a general heading because it introduces the entirety of what is to be explained.
The root text says: "What are the ten? First, one shall be protected and remembered by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions."
Second, one cannot be terrified by various māras or evil spirits. Third, one cannot be deluded or disturbed by the ninety-five kinds of externalists, ghosts, or spirits.
Fourth, one remains far removed from slandering the profound Dharma, and heavy karmic obstacles gradually diminish.
Fifth, one extinguishes all doubts and all evil discursive thoughts. Sixth, regarding the Tathāgata...
1. Faith increases as one encounters various objects of experience. 2. One remains far removed from sorrow and affliction. 3.
Within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one is courageous and undaunted. 4. One’s mind becomes gentle and supple; having abandoned arrogance, one is not troubled by others. 5.

Although one has not yet attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), at all times and in all circumstances, one is able to diminish and suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*) and takes no pleasure in them.
The World. Tenth: if one attains samādhi, one is not startled or disturbed by any external conditions or sounds. The commentary states:
Within this section on the gate of general exposition, there are two gates. First is the gate of the general inquiry, because it inquires generally into that which is taught.
Second is the gate of the specific exposition, which contains ten kinds of supreme and wondrous merits accomplished through a single true concentration.
First, the merit of protection, because one is constantly protected and remembered by all the infinite and boundless Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
second, the merit of terrifying Māra, because one is able to effectively subdue all Māras;
third, the merit of exiting the path, because one is able to effectively transcend all non-Buddhist paths and heterodox ways; fourth, the merit of being free from slander.
1. The merit of being able to skillfully distance oneself from transgressions such as slandering the Mahāyāna; 2. The merit of generating joy and faith toward the supreme and wondrous objects. 5.

The merit of resolving doubts, because one is able to skillfully cut through all forms of uncertainty. 6. The merit of profound faith, which gives rise to a joyful and confident mind regarding the sublime and excellent realms.
7. The quality of valor: Because it becomes even more profound, one gives rise to great compassion toward the realm of sentient beings and accumulates the myriad practices without indolence.

8. The quality of selflessness: Because one is able to skillfully eliminate all mental engagements of pride (*māna*), which are the pure intentions of the Buddha-dharma. 9. The quality of renunciation: At all times...
Within various objective spheres such as the sense bases, one is able to effectively subdue and eliminate the manifold afflictions;
because one has abandoned the worldly ocean of birth and death, there are ten qualities of tranquility. Regarding all objects of distraction, the mind remains stable and unmoving;
this may be understood according to the sequence of the text.
The text states: Furthermore, if a person practices only *śamatha*, the mind will become sunken or indolent;
they will take no delight in various virtues and remain far removed from great compassion. Therefore, one must practice *vipaśyanā*.

The Commentary states: This explains the gates of benefit and loss regarding the presence or absence of the two wheels. There are six such gates: first, the gate showing the faults of lacking the wheel of *śamatha* (calm abiding);
second, the gate displaying the practice of the wheel of *vipaśyanā* (insight); third, the gate establishing vows based on the realm of sentient beings;
fourth, the gate of the non-separation of the two wheels as they turn together; fifth, the gate displaying the objects to be remedied by the two wheels; sixth, the general... [text truncated].
This concludes the section on the gate of the simultaneous turning of both wheels. Within this first gate, there are four faults.
First is the fault of sinking and stagnation: the mind is dull and obscure, unable to achieve clear realization, like a person rubbing a key in a dark room.
First, the fault of mental sinking: because the mind becomes despondent, as in the case of the inhabitants of Arbuda. Second, the fault of lack of diligence:
because the mind is indolent and unable to exert effort, as in the case of the inhabitants of Aparagoyānī. Third, the fault of turning away from the wholesome:
because the mind is one-pointed and cannot discriminate between what should and should not be done, as in the case of the inhabitants of Uttarakuru.
Because they are like corpses; as it says in the original text, because they do not delight in various virtues. Fourth, there is the fault of being devoid of compassion:

their minds are tranquil and still, yet they are unable to give rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), just as one whose sense faculties are impaired does not increase further in what they personally desire.
As it says in the original text, because they are far removed from great compassion. Therefore, for one who practices contemplation, this is precisely the simultaneous operation of contemplation.
The text states: "One who practices contemplation should observe that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world cannot endure for long and must inevitably undergo change and decay.
All mental activities arise and perish from moment to moment; for this reason, they are suffering."

The Treatise says: This demonstrates the gateway of the wheel of contemplative practice (*bhāvanā-cakra*). This gateway has three parts: first, the gateway of contemplating the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*);

second, the gateway of contemplating impermanence (*anityatā*); and third, the gateway of contemplating impurity (*aśubhā*). Regarding the first, the contemplation of the characteristic of suffering, there are two types:
first, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). This refers to all pure conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) which are capable of destroying all that is impure.
Furthermore, because all impure phenomena (*aśubha-dharma*) are able to destroy all pure phenomena (*śubha-dharma*).
Moreover, because two kinds of worlds mutually destroy one another: first, the world endowed with all [conditions];
second, the world of conditioned existence characterized by false appearances (*nimitta*). Since these two kinds of worldly phenomena are mutually destructive, it is therefore said:
It is said that this refers merely to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*). If one cultivates this contemplation, what benefit will be gained?
It is the accomplishment of two profound dharmas: first, [the realization] that one is made by oneself; and second, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkha*).

This means that all mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) constantly and perpetually shift from moment to moment, arising and ceasing with extreme rapidity, such that they cannot remain in this place and move to another.
The root text says: "One should contemplate all dharmas remembered in the past as being as fleeting and insubstantial as a dream.

One should contemplate all dharmas remembered in the present as being like a flash of lightning. One should contemplate all dharmas remembered in the future as being like floating clouds that suddenly arise."
The Treatise says: This explains the gate of contemplating impermanence. There are three kinds. First, the impermanence of what has already passed:
past phenomena existed previously but are now non-existent, just as a dream exists while one is fast asleep but is no longer present once one has awakened.
Second, the impermanence of what currently exists: present phenomena did not exist in the past but exist now, just like lightning.
The light immediately extinguishes; because it cannot remain for long, there will be impermanence.
Third, all future phenomena lack intrinsic nature and arrive suddenly, like floating clouds that do not know where they come from yet suddenly arise, pervading the ten directions.
The *Mūla* says: "One should contemplate that all bodies existing in the world are entirely impure and defiled in various ways; not a single one is worth delighting in.

The *Śāstra* says: "This explains the gate of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). That is to say, taking various bodies as objects, one forms the understanding of them as impure and thereby distances oneself [from attachment]."
Because of greed.

The original text says: "One should reflect in this way: Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have been perfumed by ignorance, which causes the mind to undergo arising and ceasing, leading them to experience all manner of great suffering of body and mind. Even in the present, there is no..."
They are oppressed by this measure; the suffering of future lives is likewise without limit. It is difficult to abandon and difficult to escape, yet they remain unaware of it.
Sentient beings in such a state are truly to be pitied.
The treatise says: This explains the gateway of establishing vows by taking the realm of sentient beings as the object.
This gateway has two parts: first, the gateway of contemplating sentient beings; second, the gateway of establishing vows that pervade everywhere. This is the first gateway.
It refers to taking all limitless and boundless sentient beings within the three realms as the object and forming this thought: "From time immemorial..."
Because they are shrouded and concealed by fundamental ignorance, they turn their backs on their own original awakening—the pure Buddha—and there will be no day they return to the source.
To emerge from the treasury of ignorance will be even more distant. If I do not give rise to compassion and take them into my care, [they will remain lost].

Furthermore, as one continues this practice, it may take many eons before the time for attaining perfect enlightenment arrives; indeed, there is no fixed limit, because one has given rise to a boundless mind of great compassion.
The original text says: Having engaged in this reflection, one should immediately and courageously establish a great vow, praying that one’s own mind be free from fragmentation.
Because they are distinct, they universally cultivate all virtuous merits throughout the ten directions;
until the end of the future, they employ immeasurable skillful means to extract all suffering and affliction from sentient beings, enabling them to attain the ultimate bliss of nirvāṇa.
The treatise says: This is the gateway for the universal distribution of established vows.

That is to say, having completed such contemplation, one immediately establishes the great vow and gives rise to prajñā-light rays as numerous as the atoms in the worlds of the ten directions, penetrating the various mental characteristics as numerous as the atoms in the worlds of the ten directions, and counteracting [the afflictions] as numerous as the atoms in the worlds of the ten directions.

Because all oceans of afflictions and karmic obstructions are completely eliminated without remainder, and because the causes for practices as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions are perfected,
and the resultant virtues as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions are fully realized.

The text says: Because such vows have been made, at all times and in all places, one practices and studies all manner of wholesome deeds according to one's capacity, never abandoning them, with a mind free from indolence.
The Commentary says: This explains the gate of the simultaneous operation of the two wheels without separation;
that is to say, having completed the arousal of such vows, one immediately and directly cultivates the ocean of causal practices.
The Root Text says: "Except when sitting and single-mindedly focusing on *śamatha*, one should in all other instances observe what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
The Commentary says: "If one gives rise to the ocean of vows but does not diligently practice, one will be unable to adorn and perfect the fruit."
The *Mūla* says: "Whether walking or standing, whether rising or lying down, one should always practice both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* together.
The *Bhāṣya* says: "If one is to practice, how should it be done? It means that the two wheels must be kept from being unbalanced."

The text states: "That is to say, although one contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unarisen, one nevertheless contemplates that through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the karmic actions of good and evil and their retributions of suffering and pleasure are neither lost nor destroyed. Although one contemplates the karmic retributions of good and evil according to causes and conditions..."
And yet, even that nature of mindfulness is unattainable.
The Treatise says: This possesses the characteristics of two wheels. In which sūtra is this clearly revealed?
It refers to the opening of the gate of one hundred and ten thousand kinds of profound, vast, and perfect dhāraṇīs initiated by Mañjuśrī.
The *Mahābodhisattva-bhadrakalpa-samudra-saṃnipāta-sūtra* states: At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what is meant by the 'gate of the simultaneous practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā without separation'?
May I and this entire ocean-like assembly of immeasurable and boundless beings all enter into the ignorance of neither-knowing-nor-perceiving."

"O Sea, we are unable to penetrate it and unable to escape from it. As is fitting, World-Honored One, we pray that you will clearly reveal it for us, your deluded children. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively; reflect upon this well. I shall analyze and explain it for you. Thereupon, the World-Honored One...
He spoke in verse:
"Just as a bird lacking wings, a chariot with but one wheel, a person missing a foot, or a horse blind in its eyes—none of these can soar to great heights;
they can only carry their burdens according to their limited capacity."
Wandering upon those paths, one does not fall into the pits of evil destinies.
Know that it is likewise for one who possesses one wheel but lacks the other;
because in reality there is no dharma-nature within the void, one soars by riding upon knowledge of things as they are, entering the ocean of the treasury of dharmas.
Carrying the jewels of principle and meaning upon the level path of True Suchness (tathatā),
they travel everywhere through all realms of Māras and non-Buddhists, as well as within the deep pits of false views;
because they do not fall headlong into these pits, all practitioners must keep both wheels fully engaged and never abandon them.
If there are practitioners who do not possess these two wheels, they will ultimately be unable to penetrate the stage of unsurpassed great enlightenment.
Now, this scriptural passage is intended to demonstrate the cultivation of samādhi to reach the state of tranquility, and the cultivation of wisdom.
Wisdom illuminates the objects of discursive movement; within stillness, it never abandons movement, and within distraction, it never abandons stillness.
Yet they do not become separated from one another, for they proceed and revolve together.

Furthermore, it is to demonstrate that while practicing samādhi one realizes emptiness and the absence of objects, one practices wisdom to illuminate the presence of the subject, remaining unattached even within emptiness.

There is existence; while abiding in existence, one is not defiled by non-existence. Existence and non-existence are both illuminated, without partiality toward either side, yet they do not abandon one another, as they proceed and revolve together.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the cultivation of samādhi and the realization of the principle of equality.

One cultivates wisdom to illuminate the diversity of phenomena. One attains simultaneous realization of both principle and phenomena, without falling into partiality, as they are neither abandoned nor separated from one another, proceeding and revolving together.
Furthermore, this is to demonstrate that *śamatha* (calm abiding) can only be established in dependence upon *vipaśyanā* (insight), and is not calm abiding by its own nature;
likewise, *vipaśyanā* can only be established in dependence upon *śamatha*, and is not insight by its own nature. It is also...

Because there is no cessation and no contemplation. Furthermore, it is to demonstrate that cessation is itself contemplation and contemplation is itself cessation, because cessation and contemplation are of one essence and without distinction. This should be carefully examined and analyzed according to their respective order.

The text states: "If one cultivates *śamatha*, it serves as an antidote to the ordinary person’s dwelling in and attachment to the mundane world, and enables the relinquishing of the timid views of the two vehicles.

If one cultivates *vipaśyanā*, it serves as an antidote to the fault of the two vehicles’ failure to give rise to great compassion and their narrow-mindedness, and brings about distance from the ordinary person’s failure to cultivate roots of goodness."

The Commentary says: This exposition reveals the gates of what is to be remedied by the two wheels. If there is a practitioner who cultivates the wheel of *śamatha*, it is for the purpose of counteracting the fault of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who cling to existence;

because both [types of practitioners]—ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*)—are completely freed from and detached from their respective faults, [the former clings to existence while the latter delight in emptiness].
If there is a practitioner who cultivates the wheel of *vipaśyanā*, it is for the purpose of counteracting the two vehicles.
Sentient beings are far removed from great compassion; they do not rescue others from the inferior faults of manifold sufferings.
These ordinary beings are perpetually indolent and incapable of diligence; they do not cultivate virtuous qualities, for they delight in the faults of evil and seek liberation from them together.
The text states: "For this reason, these two gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā mutually assist and complete one another; they do not abandon or depart from each other.
If śamatha and vipaśyanā are not possessed together, then there is no way to enter the path to bodhi."

The Commentary says: This statement summarizes the gate of the simultaneous operation of the two wheels. That is to say, it summarizes what has been explained above, because there is a great fault in the deficiency of the practitioner’s wheel.
The *Ben* (Main Text) says: "Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma...
The *Lun* (Commentary) says: "This explains the gate of encouraging the inferior to turn toward the superior and not regress. Within this, there are six [sections]: 1.
The gate of revealing the teachings studied by the provisional person; 2. The gate of the place of aversion and the regression of faith; 3. The skillful means of the Tathāgata..."

The Gate of Excellence. Fourth, the Gate of Attaining a Superior and Sublime State through the Power of Support. Fifth, the Gate of Attaining a Good Destination and Remaining Firmly Established Without Regressing.
Sixth, the Gate of Citing Sūtras to Validate One’s Own Exposition. This is the first [of the six]. Regarding the phrase "those who incline toward the provisional person":
this refers to those inferior beings who have attained the four types of mind prior to the stage of the Ten Faiths, yet have not further advanced.

Therefore, as stated in the original text, "Furthermore, because of sentient beings," it says that those who take refuge in the Dharma of what is realized are sentient beings of the lower grade within the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
They take refuge in the profound and boundless Mahāyāna at the beginning of their training;

that is to say, they take refuge in that which is the teacher of all Buddhas, which is immovable throughout the three periods of time, unchanging through the four phases, spontaneously and eternally abiding on the ground.
Because it is a great highway upon the ground before one; because one originally studied this Dharma at the outset.

The original text says: "Those who seek right faith but whose minds are timid and weak, dwelling in this Sahā world, fear that they cannot always encounter the Buddhas to personally receive and make offerings to them; they dread that the mind of faith will be difficult to accomplish. [They] desire...
Regarding "regression," the treatise says: This refers to those who regress from the gate of faith due to their aversion toward the locus [of practice].

Although those sentient beings at the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are personally able to hear and receive the extremely profound Dharma-gates, because their mental faculties (*citta-indriya*) are exceedingly inferior, they fear the two great matters.
They are unable to advance further because they are prone to regression. This single land—namely, this Sahā world—is a place of coarse conditions and the turbidity of sentient beings;
therefore, it is extremely difficult to give rise to a pure mind for the sake of diligent practice.
Why is this? Because within that mind, adverse objects are constantly and perpetually present at all times and in all places, never being relinquished from the face of the advancing mind.

Second, regarding the superior conditions: in this world, where both the environment and its inhabitants are turbid and chaotic, the appearance of Buddhas in the world is extremely rare, and immeasurable Bodhisattvas respond only to the call of those who are ready.

The time interval is extremely long. Because the appearance of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the world accords with whether the realm of the pure mind is pure or impure, for this reason, those practitioners do not encounter superior conditions; due to extreme fear, they merely give rise to the intention to retreat.

The Text says: "One should know that the Tathāgata possesses supreme skillful means to gather and protect those with faith; this refers to the causal condition of mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded intent.
The Commentary says: "This is the extraordinary gate of the Tathāgata’s skillful means; it means that all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess inconceivable..."

Because it deliberates upon the profound, most wondrous, and great skillful means (*upāya*), it is able to skillfully sustain and protect that person’s faith, causing them to progress toward ever-greater excellence.
What is called "excellent and wondrous skillful means"? It refers to the skillful means of single-mindedly recollecting the Tathāgata.

What is meant by "single-minded recollection"? It means focusing one's attention to mindfully recollect the various environments and inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*) of the pure lands in other directions. As for that recollection:
Because it causes the continuity [of the lineage] not to be severed.
The *Mūla* says: "One is born in a pure land of another direction according to one's vow.
The *Śāstra* says: This is the gate of attaining a superior and wondrous place by relying on power; for the methods of all Tathāgatas are inconceivable.
By the power of this [practice], one attains rebirth in the Land of Wondrous Joy in accordance with one's own vow.
The *Root Text* says: "One constantly sees the Buddha and is freed from the evil realms.
The *Commentary* says: This is the gate of certain non-retrogression for attaining a virtuous destination; it means that once born in that land, one beholds the Tathāgata with one's own eyes.
He possesses the marks of excellence. Having heard the profound and wondrous sounds of the holy teachings, he is forever free from ill repute.
His mind is unmoving within the ocean of meditative concentration, his body is pure and bright, and because both the primary and secondary elements are purified, he is thus serene.

The text states: As it is said in the Sūtras, if a person single-mindedly contemplates Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and dedicates the roots of goodness they have cultivated with the vow to be born in that world, they will immediately attain birth there.

Because they constantly behold the Buddha, they shall never fall back. If one contemplates that Buddha’s Dharmakāya of True Suchness and practices diligently and constantly, one will ultimately attain [birth].
Because one is born and abides in right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
The treatise says: This citation of a sūtra serves as proof for the gateway of the author's own exposition.

That is to say, it encompasses the phrasing of the original sūtra through a discourse on its characteristics and associations; it praises the explanatory text of the author's own exposition because the characteristics described in the cited sūtra text are clear.
No further commentary is required.
The original text states: "The section on practicing with faith has already been explained. Next, the section on the benefits of encouraging practice will be explained.
Thus, I have already provided a general exposition of this Mahāyāna, the secret treasury of all Buddhas."

The Commentary states: Within this passage there are eight sections. First, the section that summarizes what was previously explained; second, the section that exhorts others by highlighting the benefits of practice;
third, the section that reveals the merit of faith through the removal of doubt; fourth, the section that demonstrates superiority by means of analogy;
fifth, the section that extols the merit of receiving and upholding [the teaching]; and sixth, the section that inspires fear by highlighting the faults of slander.

Section One: The Gate of the Extensive Explanation of the Sevenfold Excellence and the Avoidance of Slander. Section Eight: The Gate of Summarizing Practice and Exhorting Others. This is the first gate;
that is to say, it summarizes the eight kinds of Mahāyāna by means of a single general term. Why are the remaining dharmas not summarized here?
It is because the root is presented in order to encompass its branches.

The text states: "If there are sentient beings who wish to give rise to right faith regarding the profound realm of the Tathāgata, to remain free from slander, and to enter the path of the Mahāyāna, they should uphold this treatise, contemplate it, and practice it; in the end, they will be able to reach the unsurpassed way."

The Commentary says: This passage exhorts people by highlighting the benefits of practicing the gateway, namely, that one may accumulate an ocean of causal practices to adorn the fruit of the Dharmakāya.
This is because one upholds this treatise, contemplates its principles, and maintains this practice constantly and continuously without interruption.

The text states: "If a person, having heard this Dharma, does not give rise to timidity or weakness, one should know that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas and will surely receive the prediction of enlightenment from all the Buddhas."
The Treatise says: This reveals the gateway of the merit of faith free from doubt.

That is to say, when sentient beings hear this Mahāyāna dharma-gate that is profoundly deep, most sublime, and vast, their minds do not harbor doubt or fear, nor do they become timid or weak, nor do they treat it with contempt or slander.
They give rise to a mind of certainty, they give rise to a firm and steadfast mind, and they give rise to...
With a heart of reverence and the arousal of loving faith, you should know that such a person is truly a son of the Buddha.

They do not sever the lineage of the Dharma, the lineage of the Saṃgha, nor the lineage of the Buddha; they maintain these continuously and perpetually, causing them to increase further and further until the end of the future.
Furthermore, they are personally prophesied by all Buddhas and are [honored] by all immeasurable Bodhisattvas.
Because of his protective mindfulness.
The original text says: "Suppose there were someone who could transform all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm, causing them to practice the ten wholesome paths;
this would not equal someone who, for the duration of a single meal, correctly contemplates this Dharma. The latter's merit exceeds the former's by an incalculable amount."
As an analogy, the treatise says: This comparison serves as a superior gateway for illustration.

That is to say, if there were someone who could skillfully gather and transform all sentient beings filling the trichiliocosm, without exception, causing them all to practice the ten wholesome paths of action; or...
Suppose there are two beings: one who, for the duration of a single meal, observes and contemplates this profound Dharma; and another.

If one were to weigh the merit of these two individuals, the merit obtained by the first person would be extremely slight and minute—like the measure of a single fragment of a mustard seed broken into a hundred parts. The merit obtained by this second person is far greater.
It is profoundly vast, like the number of atoms produced by pulverizing the worlds of the ten directions.

The original text says: Furthermore, if a person receives, maintains, contemplates, and practices this treatise, the merit they possess for even one day and one night is immeasurable, boundless, and cannot be fully described. Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were each...
Even if one were to praise their merits for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one could never exhaust them.
Why is this? Because the merits of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are inexhaustible; the merits of this person are likewise thus, having no limit.
The Commentary says: This section sets forth the gate of praising the merit of receiving and upholding [this treatise].

That is to say, if there is a person who receives and upholds this treatise and contemplates its meaning and principles for even one day or one night, the merit obtained therein will be immeasurable and boundless.

It is ineffable and inconceivable. Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and all the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and three periods of time, were each to use tongues as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions, and were each to praise it for as many unspeakable eons as there are atoms in the worlds of the ten directions; even so—
The merits possessed by such a person cannot be fully exhausted. Why is this? Because the merits of the Dharmakāya and True Suchness are equal to the realm of empty space and are without limit.
How much less could ordinary beings or those of the Two Vehicles ever praise them adequately?
Even for a person who upholds [this teaching] for no more than a single day and night, the merit obtained is still immeasurable.
It is inconceivable; how much more so if one upholds, recites, contemplates, and examines it for two days, three days, four days, or even for a hundred days.
This is because it is the most inconceivable among the inconceivable and the most ineffable among the ineffable.

The root text says: "If there are sentient beings who, within this treatise, slander it and do not believe, they shall undergo the retribution for their sins for immeasurable kalpas, enduring great suffering and affliction."
The treatise says: This sixth section is the gateway for instilling fear by raising the fault of slander.
It means that there are sentient beings who, regarding this teaching of the treatise, give rise to a lack of faith; they destroy it through slander and do not practice it.
Because the retribution for the sins incurred by such sentient beings consists of the most grievous of sufferings throughout unspeakably unspeakable eons, [this gateway is established].

The text says: "For this reason, sentient beings should simply rely on faith; they should not engage in slander, for it deeply harms themselves and also harms others, severing the seeds of the Triple Gem."
The Commentary states: This concludes the preceding section on definitive discernment (*viniścaya*).

It exhorts the practitioner that from this point onward, the causes and conditions shall be established to demonstrate grave faults—namely, that within this Dharma, those who lack faith and engage in slander lose their own roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).
This diminishes the merit of others and severs the seeds of the Three Jewels, for there will be no period of continuity.
The original text states: "Because all Tathāgatas attain nirvāṇa by relying on this Dharma;
because all Bodhisattvas practice by means of it and thereby enter the Buddha-wisdom."
The Commentary says: This seventh section, the "Extensive Explanation of the Door of Avoiding Slander," is distinguished as follows:
It means that all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the three periods of time have the Mahāyāna as their fundamental basis for attaining perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, all the immeasurable Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time likewise have the Mahāyāna as their fundamental basis for [their attainment]. It is complete.
Because of the ocean [of the Dharma], such profound and deep Mahāyāna teachings— if there are sentient beings who give rise to a lack of faith,
engage in contentious debate, and slander them— such sentient beings are also said to sever all Buddhas,
to sever all Bodhisattvas, and to cut off the Tathāgatagarbha’s original awakening (primal enlightenment).
The text states: "One should know that past bodhisattvas have already attained pure faith by relying on this Dharma;
present bodhisattvas are now attaining pure faith by relying on this Dharma; and future bodhisattvas shall attain pure faith by relying on this Dharma."
Therefore, sentient beings should diligently practice and study.
The Commentary says: This is a concluding summary of the section on exhorting people to practice; one should examine and discern it with care.
The Root Text says:
The profound and vast meaning of all Buddhas, I now proclaim in summary according to my capacity;
May this merit, like the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), Universally benefit the entire realm of sentient beings.
The commentary states: This is the "Gate of Pervasive Dedication. Within this single verse, there are three gates: first, the summary of what preceded.
There are three summarized gateways: first, the gateway of the summary of what has been taught; second, the gateway of unfolding and expanding the merits so they may become vast;

and third, the gateway of bestowing universal benefit upon sentient beings. Regarding the first gateway, there are two parts: first, the gateway that universally subsumes all that was previously taught;

and second, the gateway that reveals the characteristics of the syllables used for exposition. These should be carefully examined in their respective order. As for the profound and vast meaning of the Buddhas:
This refers to the comprehensive inclusion of all the previously explained gates; that is to say, it universally encompasses the thirty-three fundamental categories of dharmas.
What is the meaning of this? When we speak of "all Buddhas," it refers to the non-dual Mahāyāna Dharma. Why is this so?
Because this non-dual Dharma, when compared to those [individual] Buddhas, possesses superior merit. (From the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Great Original Text)
A sūtra states: "The Perfectly Round Ocean (Pariniṣpanna-sāgara) excels all Buddhas; for no Buddha can achieve that which is inferior to the Perfectly Round Ocean.

If this is so, why does the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* state that Vairocana Buddha takes the threefold world as his body and mind, and that these threefold worlds encompass all phenomena without exception? That Buddha...

Furthermore, there is nothing that the body and mind do not encompass. Although Vairocana Buddha encompasses the three worlds, because he both encompasses and does not encompass them, there is no fault.
As for what is called "profound," it refers to the fundamental dharma of the two layers of the eightfold Mahāyāna.
For what reason is it named "profound"? It is because these two layers of Mahā... [text continues].
The Mahāyāna Dharma is called "profound" because its gates of entry are expected to be extremely deep; for this reason, it is designated with the term "profound.
This should be carefully examined and discerned. As for the meaning of "vast," it refers to the two successive gates of entry into the Dharma.
Because they are established according to my own [Mahāyāna] principles, they are termed the "vast meaning. These two successive gates of entry into the Dharma each, individually, are capable of...

It extensively [elucidates] its own dharma and is able to greatly [elucidate] its own dharma; because it serves as the name and meaning for its own dharma, it establishes the designation "vast and great" (*vaipulya*) based on this principle.
When it says, "I shall now provide a general explanation according to my capacity," this demonstrates the gateway of the wheel of syllables (*akṣaracakra*) that can expound:
namely, that by means of a single comprehensive syllable, one universally upholds all various forms of exposition.
In the section on the Establishment of the Thesis (*siddhānta-vibhāga*), the term "Mahāyāna" serves as the general heading; this is precisely what is meant here.
Why does a single word encompass all these explanations? It is because it is intended to reveal that the *Mahāyāna-śāstra* is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).

Regarding the statement, "Dedicate this merit according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)," this refers to the gateway of expanding and unfolding merit—that is, the merit produced by one's own actions.
Because virtue is dedicated toward three points: first, suchness; second, the single-mind dharma; and third, original enlightenment buddha-nature.
For what reason is it dedicated toward these three? It is said that one dedicates [virtue] to suchness in order to cause the merits one has performed to become equal;
one dedicates [virtue] to the single mind in order to cause the merits one has performed to become vast.
The Dharma. Desiring to make one's own cultivated merits clear and manifest, one dedicates them toward original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
One should know it thus; one should contemplate it thus; one should dedicate it thus. What benefit is there in such dedication? It is because they are manifold. What is the meaning of this?
For example, suppose one were to take a single atom and place it within the great earth; the atom so placed would be compared to that great [earth].
The earth and so forth are without distinction; the dharma-gate of dedication is likewise. Furthermore, it is like taking a single stream of water and placing it within the great ocean:
the stream of water placed therein is equal to and indistinguishable from that great ocean;
the dharma-gate of dedication is likewise. Furthermore, it is like breaking open a small portion of space: it is immediately equal to the vast emptiness of space.
There is no distinction, for the dharma-gate of dedication is likewise so.

To speak of "universally benefiting the entire realm of sentient beings" refers to the gate of universal benefit bestowed upon sentient beings; that is to say, by raising up vast and perfect merit to pervasively benefit the realm of sentient beings.
The Great Being, with a joyful and sincere heart, exhorted the ocean-like assembly of immeasurable Buddha-sons.

I have already transcended the "hair-tip" and "three-cornered" stages; having passed beyond the four roots of birth and death, the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa has reached its full completion, and I have now begun the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa by entering the state of non-arising.
As is fitting for you, sons of the Buddhas: Having already taken the mirror of the original Śākya in both your left and right hands,
Behold the defilements of the six sense-objects upon the face of the seven consciousnesses’ distracted thoughts,
And wash away the faults of clinging to phenomena and the self.
O sons of the Buddha, if you are thus, The three bodies—the Dharma-body, the Sambhoga-body, and the Nirmāṇa-body—will manifest perfectly before you like the syllables A, U, and Ma;
The four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity will be fully produced within you like entering a pond of lotuses. I have come from the sovereign realm of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Descending into the dragon palaces of the great ocean, he surveyed, according to his capacity,
the ocean of various sūtras, totaling one hundred lakṣas in number. Within the formal presentation of the Mahāyāna-śāstra,
he established the true Dharma of these sūtras and their immeasurable, boundless, and diverse meanings.
This is the summary, the formal establishment, and the complete exposition:
If there is a son or daughter of good family who holds this treatise in their own hands, they are called one who "holds a hundred lakṣas of sūtras";
if they recite the root sections from their own mouth, they are called one who "recites a hundred lakṣas of sūtras."

The merit obtained by this person— though all the Buddhas and the great assembly of Bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions were each to extend as many tongues as there are atoms in a world-system,
and were to praise it without ceasing for as many eons as there are such atoms— they could not exhaustively describe it.
How much more so for those who examine its principles and contemplate the meanings expressed within its words—
those sons and daughters of good family who give rise to a lack of faith and slander this treatise;
the karmic offenses incurred by such persons are as numerous as the atoms of dust in the worlds of the ten directions.
The Buddhas and the assembly of great Bodhisattvas each extend tongues as numerous as motes of dust;
even if they were to speak without ceasing for as many eons as there are such motes of dust,
they could not exhaustively describe this person’s past transgressions, which no Buddha can save.
Therefore, practitioners should return to the source; They ought to rely on this treatise and practice accordingly.
One must never give rise to a lack of faith Or slander the profoundly deep Mahāyāna teachings.
May this exhortation spread far and wide, Pervading throughout the myriad, overlapping Buddha-lands.
This is a brief commentary on the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*,
compiled by collating it with the Ishiyamadera manuscript.
